findings.quote: Acyclicity rules out an arrow from the last vertex back into the path.
findings.problem: The paragraph claims that each hypothesis has a visible job, and then lists nonemptiness, finiteness and acyclicity. The fourth hypothesis, 'oriented', has no job at all, and an attentive student will ask what it does. In fact acyclic already implies oriented, because u->v->u is a directed cycle with two steps. The theorem therefore holds for every nonempty finite acyclic directed graph, and the text never says so.
findings.fix: Append after this sentence: "The word ``oriented'' adds nothing to the theorem: in an acyclic directed graph no two vertices are joined in both directions, because $u\to v\to u$ would be a directed cycle with two steps. So every nonempty finite acyclic directed graph has a sink. We state the theorem for oriented graphs because those are the graphs of Section~\ref{ch07:sec:seymour}."

findings.quote: A directed path never repeats a vertex, so it lists at most $|V|$ vertices. The finite set $V$ allows only finitely many lists of at most $|V|$ different vertices, so the graph has only finitely many directed paths. It has at least one: since the graph is nonempty, we can pick a vertex, and a single vertex is a directed path of length $0$. The lengths of the directed paths therefore form a nonempty finite set of natural numbers, which has a largest member.
findings.problem: The step 'only finitely many lists of at most |V| different vertices' is asserted without a reason. A beginner cannot fill it in, since it needs a counting argument such as |V|^l lists of length l. The proof only needs the lengths to be bounded, and that is immediate. Bounding the lengths removes the unexplained step and shortens the proof.
findings.fix: Replace with: "A directed path never repeats a vertex, so it has at most $|V|$ vertices, and its length is at most $|V|-1$. The graph has at least one directed path: since the graph is nonempty, we can pick a vertex, and a single vertex is a directed path of length $0$. So the lengths of the directed paths form a nonempty set of natural numbers, none larger than $|V|-1$. Such a set is finite, so it has a largest member (as in Section~\ref{ch05:sec:euclid})."

findings.quote: Being a king does not settle that comparison (Exercise~\ref{ex:7.6}), so the two questions should be kept apart, even though they sound alike.
findings.problem: This gives away the answer to transfer Exercise 7.6, which asks 'Does it follow that |N_2^+(v)| >= |N_1^+(v)|?'. The closing clause is also mildly preachy.
findings.fix: Replace with: "The two questions sound alike, and Exercise~\ref{ex:7.6} asks you to decide whether being a king settles the comparison."

findings.quote: Look back at where the proof used the word ``simple.'' The group of an edge has exactly two members because the two endpoints of an edge are different. The group of a vertex $v$ has exactly $\deg(v)$ members because of the second reading of the degree, which needed both halves of ``simple.''
findings.problem: This is padding. It repeats the proof's own two justifications ('These are two different pairs, because $u\ne w$' and 'As Section 7.1 showed, there are exactly deg(v) such edges'). It also repeats the 7.1 paragraph that already explains why both conditions of 'simple' are needed. It sits between the proof and the next result and delays the main line.
findings.fix: Delete the whole paragraph. The proof and the paragraph in Section 7.1 ('Both halves of the word ``simple'' are needed here...') already make the point.

findings.quote: Notice how little the proof needed to know about $u$. It did not use $u$'s results against any players outside $A$ and $v$. If neither way of reaching $u$ works, $u$ must have beaten all $|A|$ members of $A$, and $v$ as well; the extra one in $|A|+1$ comes from $v$, which is not counted in $A$. That alone gives $u$ more wins than $v$. The extremal choice of $v$, a vertex with as many wins as anyone, is exactly what turns ``$u$ has more wins than $v$'' into a contradiction.
findings.problem: This paragraph re-runs the last half of the proof that was just read ('u beat every member of A, and it also beat v, which is not a member of A ... at least |A|+1'). Only the first and last sentences add anything.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Notice how little the proof needed to know about $u$: only its results against $v$ and against the members of $A$. Those results alone give $u$ more wins than $v$, and the extremal choice of $v$, a player with as many wins as anyone, turns this into a contradiction."

findings.quote: In September 2026, a preprint claiming a proof of the full conjecture was released, together with a formal proof in the Lean proof assistant, in OpenAI's public mathematics repository~\cite{oai173}.
findings.problem: 'Preprint' is used here for the first time in the book and is not defined until Chapter 17 (Section 17.8). 'Formal proof' is also unexplained at this point. A first-year student reading alone will not know either term.
findings.fix: Replace with: "In September 2026, a \emph{preprint} (a research paper made public before a journal has reviewed it) claiming a proof of the full conjecture was released in OpenAI's public mathematics repository~\cite{oai173}. It came with a \emph{formal proof}: a version of the proof written in the language of the proof assistant Lean, so that a computer program can check every step."

findings.quote: In words, $w$ belongs to $N_2^+(v)$ when it can be reached from $v$ in two steps but not in fewer. It is not $v$ itself, which is at distance $0$, and it is not a first out-neighbor, which is at distance $1$, but some directed walk $v\to u\to w$ of length $2$ reaches it. So $N_2^+(v)$ is exactly the set of vertices at directed distance \emph{exactly} two from $v$.
findings.problem: The same characterization is stated twice in three sentences, and 'distance exactly two' doubles 'exactly'. The term 'two-step route' is used as a technical term from the next paragraph on ('the two-step routes from $a$ are', 'counted two-step routes instead of vertices') but is never defined. Earlier, 'route' was used only informally. The notation $v\to u\to w$ used as a condition (meaning both $v\to u$ and $u\to w$) is also never spelled out.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Here $v\to u\to w$ means that both $v\to u$ and $u\to w$ are directed edges; we call such a directed walk of length $2$ a \emph{two-step route} from $v$. In words, $w$ belongs to $N_2^+(v)$ when some two-step route from $v$ ends at $w$ but no shorter walk reaches it: $w$ is not $v$ itself (distance $0$) and not a first out-neighbor (distance $1$). So $N_2^+(v)$ is exactly the set of vertices at directed distance two from $v$."

findings.quote: Which players are kings, and must there be one at all? An extremal choice answers the second question.
findings.problem: The first question is raised and never answered. The Pause only treats $s$. A student checking will find that p, q and s are kings and r is not, but the text never confirms this or shows a non-king. A non-king is a useful contrast.

Then extend the Pause check (line 40) after "...and $s$ is a counterexample." with: "Not every player is a king, however: $r$ beat only $s$, and $s$ beat only $p$, so $r$ cannot reach $q$ within two steps. It also describes the extremal choices only as 'shortest or longest', although Section 7.6 chooses a vertex of maximum outdegree.

Choose an object that is as short, as long, or as large as possible, and use that choice to force useful structure."

findings.quote: So we can split the degree sum into two parts: the sum $S_{\mathrm{even}}$ of the even degrees and the sum $S_{\mathrm{odd}}$ of the odd degrees.

(In the example graph, $S_{\mathrm{even}}=\deg(a)+\deg(b)=4$ and $S_{\mathrm{odd}}=\deg(c)+\deg(d)=4$.)"

findings.quote: Both totals count the same eight entries, so they must agree. Nothing was counted differently: the same entries were grouped in two different ways.
findings.problem: Redundant: the second sentence restates the first.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Both totals count the same eight entries, grouped in two different ways, so they must agree."

findings.problem: This is a filler preamble before the point.
findings.fix: Replace with: "This is no accident, and the small case already shows why."

findings.fix: Replace with: "This is the case $k=1$, and it is the one used most often."

findings.quote: It does not follow that every vertex has degree $2m/n$, or even a degree close to it.

findings.quote: Since edges have no direction, reading a walk backward gives a walk in the opposite direction: $d,c,a$ is a walk from $d$ to $a$. We call two vertices \emph{connected} when there is a walk from one to the other.
findings.problem: A definition is tucked into the end of an example paragraph. The text never says why 'from one to the other' needs no direction, even though the reversal remark just before it is exactly the reason.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Since edges have no direction, reading a walk backward gives a walk in the opposite direction: $d,c,a$ is a walk from $d$ to $a$. So if there is a walk from $u$ to $w$, there is also one from $w$ to $u$, and we simply call $u$ and $w$ \emph{connected}."

findings.quote: An object chosen to be as small or as large as possible in some measured respect is called \emph{extremal}
findings.problem: 'In some measured respect' is stilted.
findings.fix: Replace with: "An object chosen to make some quantity, such as a length, as small or as large as possible is called \emph{extremal}"

findings.quote: The next two sections give two more examples, a longest path and a vertex with as many outgoing edges as possible.
findings.problem: 'Path' was just defined for undirected graphs, but the next section uses a longest directed path.
findings.fix: Replace with: "The next two sections give two more examples: a longest directed path, and a vertex with as many outgoing edges as possible."

findings.quote: In this section the set of vertices is allowed to be infinite, and we say ``finite'' explicitly whenever a result needs it.
findings.problem: The definition of directed graph is used throughout the book (Sections 7.7, 17.7, Chapter 16), so 'In this section' is too narrow.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Unlike a graph, a directed graph may have infinitely many vertices, and we say ``finite'' explicitly whenever a result needs it."

findings.quote: A graph with no vertices has no sink, simply because it has no vertices at all.
findings.problem: The sentence is circular in wording, and 'graph' should be 'directed graph' here.
findings.fix: Replace with: "A directed graph with no vertices has no sink, since a sink is a vertex."

findings.quote: Choose a vertex $v$ of maximum outdegree, and let $A$ be the set of its out-neighbors
findings.problem: The proposition claims that *every* vertex of maximum outdegree is a king. 'Choose a vertex' suggests a particular choice rather than an arbitrary one.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Let $v$ be any vertex of maximum outdegree, and let $A$ be the set of its out-neighbors"

findings.quote: So a king need not have maximum outdegree. The proposition gives a sufficient condition for being a king, not a necessary one. Its converse, ``every king has maximum outdegree,'' is false, and $s$ is a counterexample.
findings.problem: Three sentences say the same thing in three ways.
findings.fix: Replace with: "So the converse, ``every king has maximum outdegree,'' is false, and $s$ is a counterexample: maximum outdegree is a sufficient condition for being a king, not a necessary one."

findings.quote: This section states a problem about directed graphs that stayed open for more than thirty years.
findings.problem: This duplicates paragraph 7 ('For decades the conjecture remained open'). The history belongs with the 1990 and 2026 dates, not in the opening line.
findings.fix: Replace with: "This section states a research problem about directed graphs." In paragraph 7, change "For decades the conjecture remained open" to "For more than three decades the conjecture remained open".

findings.quote: Indeed, $d$ is a sink, and a sink always satisfies the inequality: it has no out-neighbors, so it has no two-step routes either, and both of its out-neighborhoods are empty.
findings.problem: This repeats almost word for word the proof of Proposition~\ref{ch07:prop:acyclic-seymour} a few paragraphs later.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Indeed, $d$ is a sink, so both of its out-neighborhoods are empty and $0\ge0$; the proof of Proposition~\ref{ch07:prop:acyclic-seymour} below shows that every sink satisfies the inequality in the same way."

findings.quote: Two small examples show how the exclusions work. In the oriented graph with edges $a\to b$, $b\to c$, $a\to c$, and $c\to d$, the two-step routes from $a$ are $a\to b\to c$ and $a\to c\to d$.
findings.problem: The four-vertex graph is the key example of the section, and Chapter 16 reuses it twice, yet it is not drawn, unlike every other example graph in the chapter. The second example (the directed cycle) shows no exclusion, so 'how the exclusions work' does not fit it.

findings.quote: In the chain $a\to b\to c$, the directed distance from $a$ to $c$ is $2$, but there is no directed walk from $c$ back to $a$ at all.
findings.problem: The example shows that a directed distance can be undefined in one direction. It does not show two defined distances that differ, which is what 'depends on the order' most naturally suggests.
findings.fix: Append: "In the directed cycle $a\to b\to c\to a$, both distances exist but differ: the directed distance from $a$ to $b$ is $1$, while from $b$ to $a$ it is $2$."

findings.quote: Chapter~\ref{ch:lean2} writes the same three conditions in Lean for an arbitrary relation between vertices.
findings.problem: This sentence says why the redundant-looking condition $w\ne v$ is kept, but it never makes that link explicit, so it reads as an unrelated forward pointer.
findings.fix: Replace with: "This is why the condition is kept in the definition: Chapter~\ref{ch:lean2} writes the same three conditions in Lean for an arbitrary edge relation, which need not be oriented."

findings.quote: The definitions in this section are what let you ask that question precisely.
findings.problem: This is a filler summary sentence after the point has been made.
findings.fix: Delete the sentence.

findings.problem: The title reads like a slogan. A student scanning the table of contents for the handshake theorem, which Chapter 13 cites, will not find it.

findings.quote: Hall's theorem adds that, for each graph, exactly one of the two kinds of certificate exists.
findings.problem: The paragraph credits Hall's theorem with facts that Chapter 8 had already established. The sufficient direction was just proved using the procedure itself. The closing claim, that the procedure can never mistake unlucky early choices for a genuine impossibility, follows directly from Proposition ch08:prop:shortage (a failed search always produces a real shortage set), not from the 'exactly one certificate' statement. Read with its 'So', the paragraph sounds circular.
findings.fix: Replace from 'Hall's theorem adds that' to the end of the paragraph with: 'Together with the necessary direction, this observation is Hall's theorem in another form: for each graph, exactly one of the two kinds of certificate exists. At least one exists, because the procedure always produces one. At most one exists, because a shortage set rules out every full assignment. The procedure also never mistakes an unlucky sequence of early choices for a genuine impossibility. Unlucky choices are repaired along augmenting paths, and a search fails only when it has found a real shortage (Proposition~\ref{ch08:prop:shortage}).'

findings.quote: If $S$ had spare tasks, this would throw away tasks that other students need.
findings.problem: This overstates the case. A non-tight S does not always cost other students needed tasks. For example, with N(a)={1,2}, N(b)={3} and S={a}, removing N(S) leaves b with task 3. The example that follows shows only that the loss can happen.
findings.fix: Replace with: 'If $S$ had spare tasks, this could throw away tasks that other students need.'

findings.quote: Either way, the spare task of the group $\{b\}$ absorbs the loss.
findings.problem: In the second scenario (a gets task 1) b loses nothing, so there is no loss to absorb. 'Either way' does not fit both cases.
findings.fix: Replace with: 'In the first case, the spare task of the group $\{b\}$ absorbs the loss of task~$2$; in the second, there is no loss at all.'

findings.quote: If $S$ is nonempty and proper, then $0<|S|<|L|$. The set $L\setminus S$ of remaining students has $|L|-|S|$ members, which is also fewer than $|L|$.
findings.problem: The inequality |S|<|L| for a proper subset is asserted without a reason, and the size of L∖S is used before it is explained. A first-year reader may not see why removing at least one element lowers the size.
findings.fix: Replace with: 'Suppose $S$ is nonempty and proper. Since $S\ne L$, at least one student lies outside $S$, so $L\setminus S$ is nonempty too. Every student lies in exactly one of $S$ and $L\setminus S$, so $|L|=|S|+|L\setminus S|$. Both terms on the right are at least $1$, so each is smaller than $|L|$: we have $0<|S|<|L|$ and $0<|L\setminus S|=|L|-|S|<|L|$.'

findings.quote: Each task is acceptable to at most $d$ students in the whole graph, so it lies on at most $d$ edges of $E_S$. Adding over the tasks of $N(S)$ gives $|E_S|\le d|N(S)|$.
findings.problem: The by-task count needs every edge of E_S to be counted exactly once in the sum over tasks of N(S), because each edge has exactly one task endpoint and that endpoint lies in N(S). Chapter 7 stresses this 'counted exactly once' check, and the by-student count states its version of it, but the by-task count leaves it out.
findings.fix: Insert before 'Adding over': 'Each edge has exactly one task endpoint, so when we add, over the tasks of $N(S)$, the number of edges of $E_S$ at each task, every edge of $E_S$ is counted exactly once.' Then continue: 'Since each of these numbers is at most $d$, this gives $|E_S|\le d|N(S)|$.'

findings.quote: see that both proofs turn on the same obstruction: a group of students who between them accept too few tasks.
findings.problem: The inductive proof never builds or meets a shortage set. It turns on tight groups (equality) and on checking Hall's condition for the smaller graphs. A reader who looks for 'the same obstruction' in the second proof will not find it stated.
findings.fix: Replace with: 'and see how each proof uses Hall's condition at its decisive step: the first to rule out a failed search, the second to show that smaller problems still satisfy the condition.'

findings.quote: A greedy procedure hands out tasks one at a time and never takes a task back, so it stops as soon as its matching is maximal, and that matching need not be maximum.
findings.problem: Chapter 8's greedy procedure goes through every student and does not detect maximality. What is true is that it can add nothing once its matching is maximal, and that it always ends with a maximal matching. The answer neither states nor justifies that fact.
findings.fix: Replace with: 'A greedy procedure hands out tasks one at a time and never takes a task back. It ends with a maximal matching: if a student is left without a task, every task that student accepts was already given away when the student's turn came, and it stays given away. That maximal matching need not be maximum.'

findings.quote: The proof was found by asking separately what each situation allows.
findings.problem: This is an unsupported historical claim about how the proof was discovered. Hall's 1935 proof was different, and the tight-set induction came later. The point being taught is about the structure of the argument, not its history.
findings.fix: Replace with: 'The proof comes from asking separately what each situation allows.'

findings.quote: Prove carefully that $N(A)=B$, treating matched and unmatched edges separately, and point out exactly where the completeness of the search is used.
findings.problem: Exercise 8.6 is a 'transfer' exercise (front matter: 'use the same ideas in a new setting or with a changed hypothesis'), but it asks for Step 2 of the proof of Proposition ch08:prop:shortage word for word: the proof already treats the matched and unmatched cases in two bullets, and the 'Why is Step 2 needed?' paragraph already says where completeness is used. A student can simply copy the text. The solution 8.6 is then a third copy of the same argument.
findings.fix:
Replace the exercise with a genuine transfer that uses (C1) and (C2) for a new conclusion: "\begin{exercise}\label{ex:8.6}Suppose that the complete search of Section~\ref{ch08:sec:search}, started at an unmatched student $x$, fails, and let $A$ and $B$ be the sets of students and tasks it reached. Prove that no augmenting path for $M$ starts at $x$. (Hint: take an alternating path $x=v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_k$ with $k\ge1$, and show one vertex at a time that its students lie in $A$ and its tasks lie in $B$.) Point out exactly where the completeness of the search is used.\end{exercise}" Replace the solution with: "\sol{8.6}{Let $x=v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_k$ be an alternating path with $k\ge1$. Its first edge is unmatched, because $x$ is unmatched, so the $m$th edge is unmatched when $m$ is odd and matched when $m$ is even. The graph is bipartite and $v_0$ is a student, so $v_i$ is a student when $i$ is even and a task when $i$ is odd. We show by induction on $i$ that $v_i\in A$ when $i$ is even and $v_i\in B$ when $i$ is odd. For $i=0$ this holds, because $v_0=x\in A$. Now suppose it holds for some $i<k$.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{$i$ is even.} Then $v_i$ is a reached student, and the edge $v_iv_{i+1}$, in the odd position $i+1$, is unmatched. By (C1), $v_{i+1}\in B$.
\item \emph{$i$ is odd.} Then $v_i$ is a reached task, and the edge $v_iv_{i+1}$, in the even position $i+1$, is matched. So $v_{i+1}$ is the owner of $v_i$, and by (C2) it lies in $A$.
\end{itemize}
In both cases the claim holds for $i+1$.

An augmenting path starting at $x$ would end at an unused task $v_k$. But every task on the path lies in $B$, and by (C2) every task in $B$ is used. So no augmenting path starts at $x$.

Completeness is used only through (C1), in the even case: it guarantees that every unmatched edge at a reached student has been followed. Without it the conclusion can fail. With $M=\{\text{Ada--}1\}$, a search from Ben that stopped after reaching task~$1$ and Ada, without inspecting Ada, would report failure, although Ben, $1$, Ada, $2$ is an augmenting path; (C1) is false at Ada, whose unmatched edge Ada--$2$ was never followed.}" (Checked: the induction uses only (C1), (C2) and the parity facts proved in Section 3. NOTE: Week 9 solution cites this exercise; see crossPartitionIssues.)

findings.quote: \begin{exercise}\label{ex:8.5}A procedure increases the size of a matching by one at every step.
findings.problem: Exercise 8.5, also labelled a transfer exercise, is fully answered in the text: the end of Section 3 ('What is preserved and what makes progress') proves |M| <= |L| with the same injective map and gives the bound of |L| flips. Section 4 and Section 5 state it again. The exercise also says 'augmentations', a word the text never defines (the text says 'flips').
findings.fix:
Replace the exercise with: "\begin{exercise}\label{ex:8.5}A procedure starts from a matching with $k$ edges and, at every step, replaces the current matching by a matching with one more edge. (a)~Explain why this fact alone does not prove that the procedure stops. (b)~Section~\ref{ch08:sec:augment} showed that a matching has at most $|L|$ edges. Show that it also has at most $|R|$ edges, and deduce that the procedure makes at most $\min(|L|,|R|)-k$ steps. Give a graph and a starting matching for which this bound is smaller than $|L|-k$.\end{exercise}" Replace the solution with: "\sol{8.5}{(a)~The fact that a quantity increases by one at every step does not by itself rule out infinitely many steps. The counter $0,1,2,3,\ldots$ increases by one at every step and never stops. To conclude that a procedure stops, we also need a ceiling that the quantity can never pass.

(b)~Each edge of a matching contains exactly one task, and no two edges of a matching contain the same task, since they would then share that task as an endpoint. So sending each edge to its task is an injective map from the matching to $R$, and a matching has at most $|R|$ edges (Section~\ref{ch03:sec:injsurj}). Together with the bound $|L|$, every matching has at most $\min(|L|,|R|)$ edges. After $m$ steps the matching has $k+m$ edges, so $k+m\le\min(|L|,|R|)$, that is, $m\le\min(|L|,|R|)-k$. In the language of Habit~5, the nonnegative integer $\min(|L|,|R|)-|M|$ decreases by one at every step, so it cannot keep decreasing forever.

For example, let two students both accept only task~$1$, and start from the empty matching, so $k=0$. Then $\min(|L|,|R|)-k=\min(2,1)-0=1$, which is smaller than $|L|-k=2$. Indeed, once one student holds task~$1$, no matching has more edges.}"

findings.quote: The search keeps track of which vertices it has \emph{reached}. When it reaches a new vertex, it also records the vertex it came from, called the \emph{predecessor} of the new vertex. To \emph{inspect} a reached student $s$ means to look at every unmatched edge $s$--$t$ and, for each task $t$ that has not been reached yet, to do the following: mark $t$ as reached with predecessor $s$; if $t$ is unused, stop, because the search has succeeded; if $t$ is used, mark its owner as reached with predecessor $t$. The search itself runs as follows.
findings.problem: Two problems for a student reading alone. (1) The word 'root' appears in step 1 ('Mark the root $x$ as reached'), and again in Sections 5 and 6, but it is never defined; it is not defined in earlier chapters either. (2) The definition of 'inspect' packs three actions and a stopping rule into one sentence with semicolons, at the densest point of the chapter.

findings.quote: Section~\ref{sec:matching-trace} carries out this search on a small example.
findings.problem: The search (reached, predecessor, inspect, backward walk) is defined in abstract terms, and the first run of it comes only in Section 5 (a failing search) and Section 6. A beginner has to hold the whole abstract procedure for two sections with no instance in front of them. A tiny run on the Ada-Ben graph, which the reader already knows, would unblock this at once and connect the search to the repair of Section 3.
findings.fix: Replace the sentence with: "For example, take the stuck matching $M=\{\text{Ada--}1\}$ of Section~\ref{ch08:sec:augment} and search from the root Ben. Inspecting Ben follows the unmatched edge Ben--$1$: task~$1$ is reached with predecessor Ben, and since Ada holds it, Ada is reached with predecessor~$1$. Inspecting Ada follows her unmatched edge Ada--$2$: task~$2$ is reached with predecessor Ada, and it is unused, so the search succeeds. Following the predecessors backward from task~$2$ gives $2$, Ada, $1$, Ben, and read forward this is the repair path Ben, $1$, Ada, $2$ of Section~\ref{ch08:sec:augment}. Section~\ref{sec:matching-trace} runs the search on a larger example." (Checked by hand: Ben's only edge Ben--1 is unmatched, and Ada's edge Ada--2 is unmatched while Ada--1 is matched.)

findings.quote: A search that follows only the routes that look promising, or that gives up when its first route is blocked, can stop while (C1) is still false. Its failure tells us nothing about the problem, because an augmenting path might use an edge that it never tried. We call a search \emph{complete} when it keeps going until every reached student has been inspected, as the search above does.
findings.problem: The definition of 'complete' is imprecise. A successful search stops as soon as it reaches an unused task, before every reached student has been inspected, so by this wording the search above (which Section 5, Chapter 9 and Appendix D call 'complete') would not be complete when it succeeds. The definition also comes last, after the idea has already been stated twice.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Both properties depend on the search not giving up early. We call a search \emph{complete} if it stops only when it has reached an unused task or has inspected every reached student, as the search above does. A search that follows only the routes that look promising, or gives up when its first route is blocked, can stop while (C1) is still false. Its failure then tells us nothing about the problem, because an augmenting path might use an edge that it never tried."

findings.quote: In that order, a matching $M$ is maximal when no matching strictly contains it. This agrees with Definition~\ref{ch08:def:maximal}. Suppose first that a matching $M'$ strictly contains $M$, and choose an edge $e$ of $M'$ that is not in $M$. The set $M\cup\{e\}$ lies inside $M'$. Removing edges from a matching cannot create a shared endpoint, so every set of edges contained in a matching is again a matching. Hence $M\cup\{e\}$ is a matching, and $e$ can be added to $M$. Conversely, if some edge $e$ can be added to $M$, then $M\cup\{e\}$ is a matching that strictly contains $M$.
findings.problem: The student is never told what is being proved. 'This agrees' is followed by two implications, about a strictly larger matching and about adding an edge, and no sentence says that together they show the two meanings of 'maximal' coincide. A beginner cannot see why proving 'M' strictly contains M implies an edge can be added' establishes agreement.
findings.fix: "In that order, a matching $M$ is maximal when no matching strictly contains it. This is the same as Definition~\ref{ch08:def:maximal}, because a matching strictly contains $M$ exactly when some single edge can be added to $M$. In one direction, if an edge $e$ can be added to $M$, then $M\cup\{e\}$ is a matching that strictly contains $M$. In the other, suppose a matching $M'$ strictly contains $M$, and choose an edge $e$ of $M'$ that is not in $M$. The set $M\cup\{e\}$ lies inside $M'$, and removing edges from a matching cannot create a shared endpoint, so $M\cup\{e\}$ is a matching: $e$ can be added to $M$."

findings.quote: Why do tight groups matter? Suppose that $S$ is tight and that a full assignment exists. The students of $S$ receive $|S|$ different tasks, all of them in $N(S)$, and $N(S)$ has only $|S|$ members. So the students of $S$ use up every task in $N(S)$, and all the other students must be served by tasks outside $N(S)$. A tight group is therefore a self-contained block. We can solve the problem for its students on their own, and then solve the problem for everyone else without the tasks in $N(S)$.
findings.problem: We are about to prove that a full assignment exists, so starting with "suppose ... a full assignment exists" looks circular to a beginner. The last sentence ("We can solve ...") also asserts what the proof still has to establish.
findings.fix: "Why do tight groups matter? Suppose that $S$ is tight. In any full assignment, the students of $S$ receive $|S|$ different tasks, all of them in $N(S)$, and $N(S)$ has only $|S|$ members. So the students of $S$ use up every task in $N(S)$, and all the other students must be served by tasks outside $N(S)$. This suggests treating a tight group as a self-contained block: solve the problem for its students using only the tasks in $N(S)$, and solve it for everyone else without those tasks. The proof below must check that both smaller problems can really be solved."

findings.quote: If $S$ is nonempty and proper, then $0<|S|<|L|$. The set $L\setminus S$ of remaining students has $|L|-|S|$ members, which is also fewer than $|L|$.
findings.problem: It is not explained why S != L gives |S| < |L|, or why |L| - |S| < |L|. A beginner may not see either step.
findings.fix: "If $S$ is nonempty and proper, then $S$ contains at least one student and misses at least one student of $L$, so $0<|S|<|L|$. The set $L\setminus S$ of remaining students has $|L|-|S|$ members, which is also fewer than $|L|$ because $|S|>0$."

findings.quote: Now suppose that Hall's condition holds but no nonempty proper group is tight. Then every such group has at least one spare task. We will see that this spare capacity makes it safe to give any student any task that student accepts.
findings.problem: Padding. The "Proof plan" paragraph that follows immediately restates this. Merging the two gets the student to the plan faster.
findings.fix: Delete this paragraph. In the Proof plan, replace "If no nonempty proper group is tight, give one student any task it accepts, and show that the smaller problem that remains still satisfies Hall's condition." with "If no nonempty proper group is tight, every such group has at least one spare task. Then give one student any task the student accepts, and show that the smaller problem that remains still satisfies Hall's condition."

findings.quote: You can check all $2^4=16$ inequalities of \eqref{eq:hall} for this graph. The group $S=\{a,b\}$ accepts exactly two tasks, so it is tight.
findings.problem: The text never says that the graph satisfies Hall's condition, only that the student "can check" the inequalities. A student who does check will also find that {a,b,c} is tight (N = {1,2,3}) and may wonder why {a,b} was chosen.
findings.fix: "This graph satisfies Hall's condition, as you can check from all $2^4=16$ inequalities of \eqref{eq:hall}. The group $S=\{a,b\}$ accepts exactly two tasks, so it is tight. (So is $\{a,b,c\}$, which accepts tasks $1,2,3$. Any nonempty proper tight group would serve, and we use $\{a,b\}$.)"

findings.quote: The prime only marks this as a new set, different from $N(T)$.
findings.problem: The phrasing is stilted.
findings.fix: "The prime is just a label that distinguishes this set from $N(T)$."

findings.quote: The same subtraction works for $T=\{c,d\}$. Together with $S$ it forms the whole class, which accepts the four tasks $1,2,3,4$. Removing the two tasks of $N(S)$ leaves $N'(T)=\{3,4\}$: two tasks for two students.
findings.problem: Padding. The paragraph repeats the T={c} computation with nothing new, and it stands between the example and its key lesson (why S∪T is used). Section 5 restates the whole-class fact on its own, so nothing depends on this paragraph.
findings.fix: Delete the paragraph.

findings.quote: That is why it applies Hall's condition to the combined group $S\cup T$ rather than to $T$ alone.
findings.problem: "That is why" has no clear antecedent. The previous sentence states a goal, not a reason.
findings.fix: "To do so, it applies Hall's condition to the combined group $S\cup T$, not to $T$ alone."

findings.quote: \emph{Induction step.} Let $n\ge1$, and assume that $P(m)$ holds for every natural number $m<n$.
findings.problem: Chapter 5 states the strong induction step as "if P(0),...,P(k) are all true, then P(k+1) is true". A student comparing the two may not see that this is the same form.
findings.fix: Append: "(This is the strong induction step of Chapter~\ref{ch:induction}, with $n$ in place of $k+1$: we assume $P(0),P(1),\ldots,P(n-1)$.)"

findings.quote: If we give $a$ task~$1$ instead, $b$ keeps both of its tasks. Either way, the spare task of the group $\{b\}$ absorbs the loss.
findings.problem: "Either way" is inaccurate, because when a takes task 1 nothing is lost. The example also never states that this graph satisfies Hall's condition, which Case 2 assumes. It would read better before "\subsection*{The inductive proof}", parallel to the Case 1 example.
findings.fix: After "Let $N(a)=\{1,2\}$ and $N(b)=\{2,3\}$." insert "The whole class accepts three tasks, so Hall's condition holds." Replace the last two sentences with: "If we give $a$ task~$1$ instead, $b$ loses nothing. When there is a loss, the spare task of the group $\{b\}$ absorbs it." Optionally move the paragraph to just before the inductive-proof subsection.

findings.quote: The proof allows us to give $a$ any task it accepts
findings.problem: The pronoun for students changes within the chapter. Section 1 uses "they" ("a task they accept", "whether they belong to it"), while Section 4 uses "it" ("any task it accepts") and also "that student".
findings.fix: Pick one convention for the chapter, e.g. "The proof allows us to give $a$ any task that $a$ accepts", and in the Proof plan "give one student any task the student accepts".

findings.quote: If $S$ had spare tasks, this would throw away tasks that other students need.
findings.problem: This is overstated. A non-tight S does not always throw away needed tasks. For example, with N(a)={1,2} and N(b)={3}, removing N({a}) is harmless. The example that follows shows only that it can happen.
findings.fix: "If $S$ had spare tasks, this could throw away tasks that other students need."

findings.quote: If Case~1 allowed $S=L$, the first smaller problem would be the original problem itself, again with $n$ students.
findings.problem: This is not quite accurate. With S=L, G_1 has right part N(L), so any task that nobody accepts is dropped. The real point is that G_1 still has n students.
findings.fix: "If Case~1 allowed $S=L$, the first smaller problem would still have all $n$ students, so the induction hypothesis would not apply to it."

findings.quote: The induction hypothesis can be applied only to graphs that satisfy Hall's condition, so a proof must show that both smaller problems satisfy it. That check is the heart of the proof, not a bookkeeping detail.
findings.problem: Padding. The same point is made three times in this section: here, then in the subsection "Applying a theorem means checking all of its hypotheses" ("The third item is where the work lies ..."), and once more in its last paragraph ("Naming the theorem is not enough; the object must actually satisfy everything the theorem demands."). The "not a bookkeeping detail" contrast is also defensive.
findings.fix: Replace the two sentences with: "It never checks that the two smaller problems satisfy Hall's condition, and without that check the induction hypothesis cannot be applied to them." Delete the final sentence of the section, "Naming the theorem is not enough; the object must actually satisfy everything the theorem demands."

findings.quote: Because $S$ is tight, these are the same tasks. The matching $M_1$ gives the $|S|$ students of $S$ different tasks, all of them in $N(S)$, and $N(S)$ has exactly $|S|$ members. So $M_1$ uses every task in $N(S)$.
findings.problem: Padding. This repeats the "Why do tight groups matter?" argument of Section 4 almost word for word, and Section 6 states it again. The new content in this answer is the second half (the tasks can be named before M_1 is found).
findings.fix: "Because $S$ is tight, these are the same tasks: the $|S|$ students of $S$ use up all $|S|$ tasks of $N(S)$, as we saw in Section~\ref{ch09:sec:inductive}." Keep the rest of the answer.

findings.quote: Many arguments begin with an inequality, and the inductive proof of Hall's theorem uses one inequality in two different ways. When $|N(S)|\ge|S|$ holds with equality
findings.problem: The opening clause is filler. Later in the paragraph, "The proof was found by asking separately what each situation allows" is an unsupported claim about how the proof was historically discovered.
findings.fix: "The inductive proof of Hall's theorem uses one inequality, $|N(S)|\ge|S|$, in two different ways. When it holds with equality". Also change "The proof was found by asking separately what each situation allows." to "The proof comes from asking separately what each situation allows."

findings.quote: The same two questions are worth asking whenever you meet a bound. Besides asking whether the bound can be improved, ask what happens when it is attained. If equality forces a recognizable structure, that structure may let you break the problem into smaller pieces. If the inequality is strict, ask how large the margin is and what it can pay for.
findings.problem: "The same two questions" refers to nothing: no two questions were posed earlier. The next sentence then brings in a third question (whether the bound can be improved), so the student cannot tell which two are meant.
findings.fix: "Whenever you meet a bound, ask whether it can be improved, and then ask two more questions. What happens when the bound is attained? If equality forces a recognizable structure, that structure may let you break the problem into smaller pieces. And when the inequality is strict, how large is the margin, and what can it pay for?" This keeps the advice that Chapter 10 and Appendix E cite.

findings.quote: The rigidity in the equality case is a familiar fact in disguise.
findings.problem: Chapter 3 states that an injective map gives |A| <= |B| and that a bijection gives |A| = |B|. It never states that an injective map between finite sets of equal size is surjective, so the fact is not "familiar" to the student. The paragraph proves it anyway.
findings.fix: "The rigidity in the equality case is a basic fact about finite sets in disguise."

findings.quote: the search followed it from $s$, so $t\in B$.
findings.problem: The model portfolio proof (9.6(c)) never says where the completeness of the search is used. It is used exactly here, and Chapter 8 stresses that completeness is the essential point. A model "complete proof" should name it.
findings.fix: Replace "If $s$--$t$ is not in $M$, the search followed it from $s$, so $t\in B$." with "If $s$--$t$ is not in $M$, then $t\in B$: the search failed, so it inspected every reached student, including $s$, and inspecting $s$ follows every edge at $s$ that is not in $M$."

findings.quote: Its edges alternate between edges not in $M$ and edges of $M$
findings.problem: The model proof asserts that the edges alternate without giving the reason.
findings.fix: "Every step into a task used an edge not in $M$, and every step into a student used an edge of $M$, so its edges alternate between edges not in $M$ and edges of $M$"

findings.quote: so it stops as soon as its matching is maximal, and that matching need not be maximum.
findings.problem: This is imprecise. A greedy procedure that halts at the first stuck student can stop at a matching that is not even maximal (e.g. N(s1)=N(s2)={1}, N(s3)={2}, processed in order s1, s2, s3). Chapter 8's wording is safer.
findings.fix: "so once no further edge can be added it is stuck at a maximal matching, and that matching need not be maximum."

findings.problem: "The table checks them directly." is a stilted, robotic closing sentence.
findings.fix: "Once this matching has been found, the necessary direction of Hall's theorem (Section~\ref{ch09:sec:necessary}) already guarantees all eight inequalities. The table confirms them one at a time."

findings.quote: For disjoint finite sets, the size of the union is the sum of the sizes (Chapter~\ref{ch:maps}).
findings.problem: The fact is stated in a specific section (Appendix E already cites it as ch03:sec:sets). A precise pointer helps the student.

findings.quote: Every output has second coordinate equal to twice the first, so the second equation never says anything that the first did not already say.
findings.problem: This is false for any target with b_2 different from 2b_1. For the target (1,0), discussed two sentences later, the second equation 2x_1+2x_2=0 contradicts the first equation x_1+x_2=1. The second equation does not just repeat the first. What is true is that its left side is always twice the left side of the first equation.
findings.fix: Replace with: "The left side of the second equation is always twice the left side of the first. So the second equation either repeats the first, when $b_2=2b_1$, or contradicts it, when $b_2\ne2b_1$. It never gives a second, independent condition on $(x_1,x_2)$."

findings.quote: Counting equations is not enough. What decides the matter is whether the map loses information.
findings.problem: "The matter" is whether two equations in two unknowns have exactly one solution, which includes existence. The previous subsection ("Uniqueness is not existence") says a zero kernel controls uniqueness only and does not guarantee that every target is reached. For square systems, a zero kernel does imply surjectivity, but the book never proves or states this. As written, the sentence suggests the kernel alone settles existence, which contradicts the earlier warning.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Counting equations is not enough. Because the kernel of this $T$ contains a nonzero vector, no target can have exactly one solution: by the description of all solutions above, each target has either none or infinitely many. Whether solutions are unique is decided by whether the map loses information, not by how many equations there are."

findings.quote: For the target $(2,4)$ there are infinitely many solutions, among them $(2,0)$ and $(1,1)$;
findings.problem: The text shows that the kernel contains one nonzero vector, (1,-1), but "infinitely many" also needs every multiple c(1,-1) to be in the kernel. A beginner may not see this step.
findings.fix: Replace with: "For the target $(2,4)$ there are infinitely many solutions. One is $(2,0)$. Since $T(c(1,-1))=cT(1,-1)=0$ for every number $c$, every vector $(2,0)+c(1,-1)=(2+c,\,-c)$ is also a solution; $c=-1$, for instance, gives $(1,1)$. The solutions $(2,0)$ and $(1,1)$ differ by $(1,-1)$, a vector in the kernel." (Then delete the now-repeated clause "these two differ by $(1,-1)$, a vector in the kernel".)

findings.quote: Splitting off one term at a time, a linear map sends every linear combination to the same combination of the outputs:
findings.problem: This extends the two-term rule to k terms by an induction that is never written out. A student with no proof experience may not see how the "splitting" works.

Splitting off one term at a time in the same way, a linear map sends every linear combination to the same combination of the outputs:"

findings.quote: In the plane, two nonzero vectors are orthogonal exactly when they are perpendicular in the usual sense. For instance, turning a vector $(a,b)$ through a right angle gives $(-b,a)$, and indeed
findings.problem: This "exactly when" claim is stated without a reason. The example only illustrates one direction, for one particular perpendicular vector. The tools for a real justification (Pythagoras and linearity) are already available.
findings.fix:
After the first sentence, add: "To see why, look at the triangle with corners $0$, $u$ and $v$. By linearity in each argument and symmetry, its side from $u$ to $v$ has squared length $
orm{u-v}_2^2=(u-v)\cdot(u-v)=
orm{u}_2^2-2(u\cdot v)+
orm{v}_2^2$. By Pythagoras' theorem and its converse, the angle at $0$ is a right angle exactly when $
orm{u-v}_2^2=
orm{u}_2^2+
orm{v}_2^2$, that is, exactly when $u\cdot v=0$." Keep the $(a,b)$, $(-b,a)$ example as an illustration.

findings.fix: Replace with: "Both are therefore nonnegative square roots of the same number $c^2\norm{u}_2^2$, and Section~\ref{ch01:sec:notation} tells us a nonnegative number has only one nonnegative square root. So they are equal."

findings.quote: So applying $A$ twice simply doubles every vector, and this one identity settles everything about $A$.

findings.problem: The inverted clause "a vector that it does make, it makes in only one way" is stilted. The reason why a(1,1)=b(1,1) forces a=b (comparing first coordinates) is also left to the reader.
findings.fix: Replace with: "The list consisting of the single vector $(1,1)$ passes the uniqueness test. Any vector it produces, it produces in only one way: if $a(1,1)=b(1,1)$, then $(a,a)=(b,b)$, and comparing first coordinates gives $a=b$."

findings.quote: These numbers crowd together, and the point they crowd around is $\sqrt2$, which is not a fraction of integers (Theorem~\ref{thm:sqrt2}). So the set $\QQ$ of rational numbers, with distance $|x-y|$, has a hole at $\sqrt2$, and it is not complete.
findings.problem: The text states as a fact that Q is not complete, but it does not prove it. "Crowd together" is never defined. The text does not show that the truncations form a Cauchy sequence. findings.fix: Replace with: "Call them $t_0,t_1,t_2,\ldots$, where $t_k$ keeps $k$ digits after the decimal point. findings.fix: Replace with: "Counting equations is not enough; we have to look at the map. Because its kernel contains the nonzero vector $(1,-1)$, no target can have exactly one solution: as soon as $x_0$ is a solution, so is $x_0+t(1,-1)$ for every real $t$."

findings.quote: Now apply this to the standard basis.
findings.problem: The fact that a linear map sends 0 to 0 is proved only inside the answer to a Pause box. Section 3 relies on it in three places: 'the kernel always contains 0', the proof of Theorem thm:kernel ('T(x)=0=T(0)'), and 'A0=0'. It even cites the pause answer as its source. A key fact should be in the main text, and it follows in one line from T(cx)=cT(x).
findings.fix: Insert a short paragraph immediately before "Now apply this to the standard basis.": "Taking $c=0$ in $T(cx)=cT(x)$ gives $T(0)=0$, because $0x$ and $0\,T(x)$ are both the zero vector. So a linear map always sends the zero vector to the zero vector." Then shorten the Pause answer (see the next finding) and change the reference in Section 3 (see the finding after that).

findings.quote: It does preserve differences, since $F(x)-F(y)=x-y$, but it moves the zero vector, and that alone rules out linearity.
findings.problem: In this chapter (and in Ch. 6), 'preserves addition' means T(x+y)=T(x)+T(y). By analogy a student will read 'preserves differences' as F(x-y)=F(x)-F(y), which is false for this F: F(x-y)=x-y+(1,0). What the text means is that F leaves the difference of two inputs unchanged.
findings.fix: Replace the whole Pause answer with: "No. A linear map sends the zero vector to the zero vector, but $F(0,0)=(1,0)$. The map $F$ is a \emph{translation}: it adds the fixed vector $(1,0)$ to every input. It leaves the difference of any two inputs unchanged, since $F(x)-F(y)=x-y$, but it moves the zero vector, and that alone rules out linearity." (If T(0)=0 is not moved into the main text, keep the existing T(0)=T(0+0) argument and change only the last sentence.)

findings.quote: The kernel always contains $0$, because a linear map sends $0$ to $0$ (see the pause question at the end of Section~\ref{ch10:sec:linearmaps}).
findings.problem: This cites a pause-box answer as the source of a fact that a theorem's proof depends on. Once T(0)=0 is stated in the main text of Section 2, a plain section reference is enough.
findings.fix: "The kernel always contains $0$, because a linear map sends $0$ to $0$ (Section~\ref{ch10:sec:linearmaps})."

findings.quote: The double sum can be hard to read, so here it is written out for two-by-two matrices.
findings.problem: The order of ideas is reversed for a beginner. The abstract triple-index regrouping with interchanged sums comes first, and the concrete 2-by-2 expansion that makes it understandable comes only afterwards, apologizing for the difficulty. Concrete should come before abstract.
findings.fix: Move the paragraph that begins "The double sum can be hard to read" (through "...in compact form.") so that it comes directly after the first paragraph of the section. Open it with: "To see what the entries of $BA$ must be, start with two-by-two matrices. The first coordinate of $B(Ax)$ is" [same display] "The coefficients of $x_1$ and $x_2$ form the first row of $BA$." Then begin the general computation with: "The same calculation works in general. Expand the $i$th coordinate of $B(Ax)$, using the row rule first for $B$ and then for $A$:" After the final formula for $(BA)_{ij}$, put the sentence "Here the index $r$ runs through the coordinates of the intermediate vector $Ax$, while $j$ runs through the coordinates of the original input $x$." Delete "The summation notation records exactly this distributive calculation in compact form."

findings.quote: Taking $x=e_j$, whose $j$th coordinate is $1$ and whose other coordinates are $0$, reduces each expression to its coefficient of $x_j$, so these two coefficients agree.
findings.problem: In both sums j is the summation index running from 1 to n, and here it is also used as a fixed index. A beginner reading sum_j (...) x_j with x=e_j cannot tell which j is which.
findings.fix: "Taking $x=e_1$ makes every term vanish except the one containing $x_1$, so the two coefficients of $x_1$ agree; taking $x=e_2$ does the same for $x_2$, and so on."

findings.quote: All the sums are finite, so this regrouping uses only the ordinary rules of arithmetic.
findings.problem: This is a defensive aside answering a worry about infinite sums, which a first-year student does not have. It also fails to say which rules are used.
findings.fix: Replace with: "The regrouping uses only the distributive law and the fact that numbers may be added in any order."

findings.quote: For an $n$-by-$n$ matrix $A$, the identity $AA^{\mathsf T}=nI$ therefore says two things at once.
findings.problem: 'Identity' here means 'equation', but two sentences earlier the same paragraph defined the identity matrix and the identity map. A beginner may read 'the identity AA^T=nI' as a statement about the identity matrix.
findings.fix: "For an $n$-by-$n$ matrix $A$, the equation $AA^{\mathsf T}=nI$ therefore says two things at once."

findings.quote: So the entries of $AA^{\mathsf T}$ are the dot products of the rows of $A$ with one another:
findings.problem: The only example of AA^T in the text is the symmetric 2-by-2 matrix A, for which A^T=A, so the transpose seems to play no role. The non-square matrix M has just been transposed, so one line would make the abstract formula concrete.
findings.fix: Before the transpose display, change "For example," to "For example, for the matrix $M$ of Section~\ref{ch10:sec:linearmaps},". After the display of $(AA^{\mathsf T})_{ij}$, add: "For this $M$, $MM^{\mathsf T}=\begin{pmatrix}14&5\\5&2\end{pmatrix}$: the rows $(2,-1,3)$ and $(1,0,1)$ have squared lengths $14$ and $2$, and their dot product is $5$." (Checked: 4+1+9=14, 2+0+3=5, 1+0+1=2.)

findings.quote: The row-by-column rule may look strange at first sight. The calculation shows where it comes from: it is exactly what composing the two maps requires.
findings.problem: Two sentences of preamble make a single point.
findings.fix: "This row-by-column rule is not an arbitrary convention: it is exactly what composing the two maps requires."

findings.quote: Each choice of $t$ gives a different inequality, and we want an informative one. A good choice removes from $u$ its part along $v$, so that what is left over, $u-tv$, is orthogonal to $v$. So we solve

findings.quote: How large can a dot product be, compared with the lengths of the two vectors? A natural guess is
findings.problem: Nothing so far makes this guess 'natural' to a beginner. One observation would motivate it.

In short, nonnegative numbers compare in the same way as their squares." Follow it with the existing two-sentence justification, then return to the example with "In our example the squares are $16$ and $10\cdot2=20$, and $16\le20$, so the guess holds."

orm{v}_2$ says that $u\cdot v$ lies between $-

orm{v}_2$ and $

orm{v}_2$.

findings.quote: This is the value of $t$ used in the proof below.
findings.problem: This repeats what the 'Plan.' line before the proof already says ('substitute the value of t found above').
findings.fix: Delete the sentence "This is the value of $t$ used in the proof below."

findings.quote: Second, the gap measures how far $u$ is from being a multiple of $v$: it equals $v\cdot v$ times the squared length of the residual.
findings.problem: This restates the displayed identity from a few lines earlier in words. Only the interpretation is new.

findings.quote: \section{Deriving a bound by removing a component}
findings.problem: The chapter's main theorem is invisible in the table of contents. A student looking for Cauchy-Schwarz (cited from Ch. 11 and Appendix E) cannot find it from this title, and 'component' is undefined when the title is read.
findings.fix: \section{The Cauchy--Schwarz inequality: removing a component}  (keep \label{ch10:sec:cs} unchanged)

findings.quote: Call a pair of different inputs with the same output a \emph{collision}. Every collision $x\ne y$ therefore produces a nonzero vector $x-y$ in the kernel. For the map $P$, the inputs $(2,5)$ and $(2,7)$ collide, and their difference $(0,-2)$ lies in $\ker P$. The kernel collects in one place all the information that $T$ cannot see.
findings.problem: The term 'collision' is defined formally but never used again in the chapter. The closing sentence ('all the information that T cannot see') is a vague metaphor, while the precise fact behind it (adding a kernel vector never changes the output) is left unsaid until Solution 10.2.
findings.fix: "So two different inputs with the same output always produce a nonzero vector $x-y$ in the kernel. For the map $P$, the inputs $(2,5)$ and $(2,7)$ have the same output $(2,0)$, and their difference $(0,-2)$ lies in $\ker P$. In the other direction, adding a kernel vector $k$ to an input never changes the output, because $T(x+k)=T(x)+T(k)=T(x)$. So the kernel records exactly the changes to an input that $T$ cannot detect."

findings.quote: At most one is not the same as exactly one: a zero kernel does not promise that every target is reached. The map $t\mapsto(t,0)$ from $\RR$ to $\RR^2$ is linear (the check is the same as for $P$), and its kernel is $\{0\}$, because $(t,0)=(0,0)$ only when $t=0$. (Here we regard $\RR$ as $\RR^1$, the lists with one coordinate.) So this map is injective.
findings.problem: 'Zero kernel' is undefined shorthand. The remark that R counts as R^1 comes after the map has already been called linear. 'So this map is injective' does not say that it follows from the theorem.
findings.fix: "At most one is not the same as exactly one: a kernel equal to $\{0\}$ does not promise that every target is reached. Regard $\RR$ as $\RR^1$, the lists with one coordinate. The map $t\mapsto(t,0)$ from $\RR$ to $\RR^2$ is linear (the check is the same as for $P$), and its kernel is $\{0\}$, because $(t,0)=(0,0)$ only when $t=0$. So this map is injective by Theorem~\ref{thm:kernel}."

findings.quote: So applying $A$ twice simply doubles every vector, and this one identity settles everything about $A$.
findings.problem: 'Settles everything about A' overclaims. The equation settles injectivity and surjectivity, which is what the paragraph then shows.
findings.fix: "So applying $A$ twice simply doubles every vector. This one equation is enough to show that $A$ is both injective and surjective."

findings.quote: Without linearity the theorem fails. The map $F:\RR\to\RR$ with $F(x)=x^2$ sends only $0$ to $0$, yet it is not injective, because $F(1)=F(-1)$.
findings.problem: F was just used for the translation in the Pause box at the end of Section 2. Reusing the letter for a different nonlinear map one page later invites confusion.
findings.fix: "Without linearity the theorem fails. The map $g:\RR\to\RR$ with $g(x)=x^2$ sends only $0$ to $0$, yet it is not injective, because $g(1)=g(-1)$."

findings.quote: In the plane, two nonzero vectors are orthogonal exactly when they are perpendicular in the usual sense.
findings.problem: This is asserted without reason. The example that follows checks only one special case (a quarter-turn). A student will ask why a zero dot product means a right angle. One sentence using Pythagoras, already used two paragraphs earlier, answers that.
findings.fix:
After this sentence (and after the (a,b),(-b,a) example), add: "To see why, multiply out the squares: $
orm{u-v}_2^2=(u_1-v_1)^2+(u_2-v_2)^2=
orm{u}_2^2+
orm{v}_2^2-2(u\cdot v)$. By Pythagoras' theorem and its converse, the triangle with corners $0$, $u$, $v$ has a right angle at $0$ exactly when $
orm{u-v}_2^2=
orm{u}_2^2+
orm{v}_2^2$, that is, exactly when $u\cdot v=0$."

findings.quote: Cancellation of exactly this kind will express the vanishing of correlations between sign sequences in Chapter~\ref{ch:signs}.
findings.problem: 'Vanishing of correlations between sign sequences' is jargon that has not been defined at this point. The sentence is a dense noun stack.
findings.fix: "Chapter~\ref{ch:signs} looks for lists of $+1$s and $-1$s that are orthogonal to their own shifted copies, and there too the positive and negative products must cancel exactly."

findings.quote: The subscript $2$ in $\norm{u}_2$ is a label for this way of measuring size, which is built from squares. It is not the second coordinate of $u$, and it does not mean that $u$ has two coordinates.
findings.problem: This notation warning comes two paragraphs after the notation was first used, after the (3,4) example and the scaling rule. A student who misreads the subscript has already been reading with the wrong idea.
findings.fix: Move the whole paragraph (through "...other ways of measuring the size of a vector.") so that it directly follows the display defining $\norm{u}_2$, and shorten its middle sentence to: "It is not a coordinate number, and it does not mean that $u$ has two coordinates."

findings.quote: Choosing a description that suits the question is a theme of this chapter, and this particular basis will return several times.
findings.problem: The subsection title promises a basis 'chosen to fit the problem', but no problem is ever posed, so the student cannot see what this basis fits. The shop example from the first paragraph supplies one at once.
findings.fix: Insert before this sentence: "For the shop's stock $(3,5)$, the coefficients are $a=4$ and $b=-1$: half the total weight $8$, and half the amount $3-5=-2$ by which flour exceeds sugar. If the shop's questions are about the total and the imbalance, this basis answers them directly." (Check: $4(1,1)-(1,-1)=(3,5)$.)

findings.quote: The definition of a basis makes two separate demands. First, every vector must have a representation, as $(3,-2)=3e_1-2e_2$ does in the standard basis. A list \emph{spans} $\RR^n$ if every vector of $\RR^n$ is a linear combination of the list. Second, the representation must be \emph{unique}: the same vector must never arise from two different lists of coefficients. A basis is a list that does both.
findings.problem: 'Representation' is used as a technical word, here and later ('two representations', 'zero vector has two different representations'), without ever being defined. 'A basis is a list that does both' is repeated almost word for word by 'In short, a basis is a list that spans and is linearly independent' at the end of the subsection.
findings.fix: "The definition of a basis makes two separate demands. First, every vector must have at least one \emph{representation}, that is, a way of writing it as a linear combination of the list, as $(3,-2)=3e_1-2e_2$ does in the standard basis. A list that meets this demand is said to \emph{span} $\RR^n$. Second, the representation must be \emph{unique}: the same vector must never arise from two different lists of coefficients." (Keep the closing 'In short...' sentence.)

findings.quote: The single vector $(1,1)$ passes the uniqueness test: a vector that it does make, it makes in only one way, because $a(1,1)=b(1,1)$ forces $a=b$.
findings.problem: The clause 'a vector that it does make, it makes in only one way' is stilted, and 'forces' skips the one-line reason.
findings.fix: "The list consisting of the single vector $(1,1)$ meets the second demand: if $a(1,1)=b(1,1)$, then $(a,a)=(b,b)$, so $a=b$."

findings.quote: So this list is not linearly independent, which is another way of saying that it does not give unique coefficients.
findings.problem: This restates what the reader established two paragraphs earlier with the two representations of (1,1).
findings.fix: "So this list is not linearly independent."

findings.quote: Let $n$ be a positive integer. A \emph{vector} in $\RR^n$ is an ordered list $x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ of $n$ real numbers, and the numbers $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ are its \emph{coordinates}. So $\RR^n$ is the set of all such lists.
findings.problem: R^n is used before it is defined, and the definition then arrives as a 'So' consequence.
findings.fix: "Let $n$ be a positive integer. We write $\RR^n$ for the set of all ordered lists $x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ of $n$ real numbers. Such a list is called a \emph{vector}, and the numbers $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ are its \emph{coordinates}."

findings.quote: Splitting off one term at a time, a linear map sends every linear combination to the same combination of the outputs:
findings.problem: 'Splitting off one term at a time' compresses a repeated use of the two-term rule. A beginner has not yet seen it done even once.
findings.fix: "Using the combined condition repeatedly, a linear map sends every linear combination to the same combination of the outputs. For three vectors, for instance, $T(a_1v_1+a_2v_2+a_3v_3)=T(a_1v_1+a_2v_2)+a_3T(v_3)=a_1T(v_1)+a_2T(v_2)+a_3T(v_3)$, and splitting off one term at a time in the same way handles any number of terms:"

findings.quote: Now apply this to the standard basis. For a linear map $T$ defined on the plane, writing $(x_1,x_2)=x_1e_1+x_2e_2$ gives
findings.problem: This is the first use of the convention of writing T(x_1,x_2) for T applied to the vector (x_1,x_2), that is, T((x_1,x_2)). The convention is never stated, and a careful beginner may wonder whether T now takes two inputs.
findings.fix: After the display that follows, add: "Here $T(x_1,x_2)$ is short for $T\bigl((x_1,x_2)\bigr)$, the value of $T$ at the vector $(x_1,x_2)$."

findings.quote: Taking $x=e_j$ shows that $Ae_j$ is column $j$ of $A$. This is why we put $T(e_j)$ in column $j$. For any linear map $T:\RR^n\to\RR^m$, build the $m$-by-$n$ matrix $A$ whose column $j$ is $T(e_j)$, for $j=1,\ldots,n$.
findings.problem: One paragraph does two jobs: it checks that the row rule equals the column combination, then builds the matrix of an arbitrary linear map. The vague bridge 'This is why we put T(e_j) in column j' hides the turn from one to the other.
findings.fix: End the paragraph after "Taking $x=e_j$ shows that $Ae_j$ is column $j$ of $A$.", delete "This is why we put $T(e_j)$ in column $j$.", and start a new paragraph: "Now let $T:\RR^n\to\RR^m$ be any linear map, and build the $m$-by-$n$ matrix $A$ whose column $j$ is $T(e_j)$, for $j=1,\ldots,n$." Keep the rest unchanged.

findings.quote: Both compositions are identity maps, so $U$ is the inverse of $T$. Both checks are needed, and each must hold at every input, not only at a few chosen ones.
findings.problem: The second sentence is a defensive aside. The computation above it is already done for an arbitrary input, so the warning answers a mistake the solution did not make.
findings.fix: "Both compositions are identity maps, so $U$ is the inverse of $T$; as in Section~\ref{ch03:sec:functions}, both checks are needed."

findings.quote: Every other completeness result we use, such as the completeness of the interval $[0,1]$ proved below, is derived from this one fact, so whenever a later argument says that a limit exists, you can trace that claim back to this assumption.
findings.problem: This is false as stated. Chapter 17 (Section ch17:sec:balls, Exercise 17.3) proves that the discrete metric on N, or on any set, is complete without using the completeness of R. Also, many limits in the book, such as 1/(n+1) -> 0, are proved directly and do not depend on completeness, so 'whenever a later argument says that a limit exists' is too broad.

So when a later argument about real numbers produces a limit without naming it in advance, that limit exists because of this assumption."

findings.quote: So the set $\QQ$ of rational numbers, with distance $|x-y|$, has a hole at $\sqrt2$, and it is not complete.
findings.problem: There is a gap. The text asserts that the truncations 'crowd together' (that they are Cauchy) and that Q is therefore not complete, but it never says why the sequence cannot converge to some other rational number. A student cannot get from 'they crowd around sqrt2' to 'no rational limit' alone. The same step is written out carefully for (0,1) a few lines later, but here it is missing.
findings.fix: Before this sentence insert: "They do form a Cauchy sequence: from the number with $k$ decimal places onward, any two of them share their first $k$ decimal places, so they differ by less than $10^{-k}$. And they cannot converge to a rational number $L$: on the real line they would then converge both to $L$ and to $\sqrt2$, so $L=\sqrt2$ by Proposition~\ref{thm:limitunique}, which is impossible." findings.fix: "This section shows that steps which shrink by a fixed factor at every stage cannot add up to much. The tool is the \emph{finite geometric sum} $1+q+q^2+\cdots+q^{r-1}$, a sum in which each term is the previous one multiplied by the same number $q$."

findings.quote: It did not need the crossing events of different edges to be unrelated, and in general they are not.
findings.problem: The book never defines "unrelated". The reader only knows independence of two events (Section 13.1). Read that way, the claim "in general they are not" is false: the crossing events of any two different edges are always independent. For disjoint edges the probability that both cross is 1/4. For edges uv and vw that share a vertex, both cross exactly when u=w differs from v, which is 2 of 8 labelings, again 1/4. The parenthesis later in the same paragraph says this itself for the triangle, so the reader is told first that the events are generally not unrelated and then that any two of them are independent. The real point is that three events can fail to multiply, and that is never made explicit: the text never says that 'all three cross' would have probability (1/2)^3=1/8 if the probabilities multiplied.
findings.fix: Replace the paragraph from "The proof used independence once" through "=3/2$." with: "The proof used independence once, to find $\Prob(A_e)=1/2$ for a single edge. It never asked how the crossing events of different edges are related to one another, and they can be linked in ways that the probabilities for single edges do not show. Consider the \emph{triangle}, the graph with three vertices $a$, $b$, $c$ and the three edges $ab$, $bc$, $ca$. As we saw for the example graph $G$, these three edges can never all cross. So the event that all three cross has probability $0$, even though each edge crosses with probability $1/2$. If the three probabilities multiplied, as the probabilities of labels on different vertices do, we would get $(1/2)^3=1/8$ instead. Any two of the three events, on the other hand, are independent: for instance, $ab$ and $bc$ both cross exactly when $a$ and $c$ get the same label and $b$ gets the other one, which happens at $2$ of the $8$ labelings, and $2/8=(1/2)(1/2)$. The link shows up only when all three edges are considered together. Linearity of expectation does not care about any of this. The expected number of crossing edges is still $1/2+1/2+1/2=3/2$."

findings.quote: \textbf{Step 6: the error bounds.} We begin with the a priori estimate. Fix $n$, and let $m$ be any index larger than $n$.
findings.problem: Step 6 proves the a priori estimate first, through an extra tolerance eta and an argument of the form A<B+eta for every eta, hence A<=B. This is the densest paragraph in the chapter. Yet if the residual estimate is proved first, the a priori estimate follows in two lines, as the pause at the end of Section ch12:sec:estimates itself shows. Reordering removes the hardest paragraph without losing any step.
findings.fix:
Replace everything from "\textbf{Step 6: the error bounds.} We begin with the a priori estimate." up to and including "...dividing by the positive number $1-q$ gives \eqref{eq:residual}. This completes the proof." with:
\textbf{Step 6: the error bounds.} We prove the residual estimate first. Let $z$ be any point of $X$. Use the triangle inequality with $Tz$ as a stop, then $x_*=Tx_*$ from Step~4, then the contraction inequality:
\[
d(z,x_*)\le d(z,Tz)+d(Tz,x_*)=d(z,Tz)+d(Tz,Tx_*)
\le d(z,Tz)+q\,d(z,x_*).
\]
Subtracting $q\,d(z,x_*)$ from both sides gives $(1-q)\,d(z,x_*)\le d(z,Tz)$, and dividing by the positive number $1-q$ gives \eqref{eq:residual}.

The a priori estimate follows by applying the residual estimate to an iterate. Take $z=x_n$. Then $Tz=x_{n+1}$, so the residual of $x_n$ is $d(x_n,x_{n+1})=d(x_{n+1},x_n)$, which Step~1 bounds by $q^nD$. Hence
\[
d(x_n,x_*)\le\frac{q^nD}{1-q}=\frac{q^n}{1-q}\,d(x_1,x_0),
\]
which is \eqref{eq:apriori}. This completes the proof.

findings.fix: Only if Step 6 is restructured, replace the whole \pauseq{...}{...} with: \pauseq{For $T(x)=(x+1)/2$ and $x_0=0$, compute the a posteriori bound for $x_n$, where $n\ge1$, and compare it with the true error $2^{-n}$.}{Here $q=1/2$, so $q/(1-q)=1$. By the formula $x_n=1-2^{-n}$, the latest step has length $x_n-x_{n-1}=2^{-(n-1)}-2^{-n}=2^{-n}$. So the a posteriori bound is $1\cdot2^{-n}=2^{-n}$, exactly the true error: in this example it cannot be improved either.}

findings.quote: \textbf{Step 4: the limit is a fixed point.} We show that the number $d(Tx_*,x_*)$ is zero.
findings.problem: The student is sent straight into an epsilon/2 argument without the one-sentence idea behind it: x_{n+1}=Tx_n, the left side tends to x_*, and the right side tends to Tx_*. Knowing the idea first makes the estimate readable.
findings.fix: \textbf{Step 4: the limit is a fixed point.} The idea is simple. Each iterate satisfies $x_{n+1}=Tx_n$. As $n$ grows, the left side approaches $x_*$, and since $T$ brings points closer together, $Tx_n$ approaches $Tx_*$. So $x_*$ and $Tx_*$ should be the same point. To prove it, we show that the number $d(Tx_*,x_*)$ is zero.

findings.quote: Notice what this argument does \emph{not} assume. It never claims that some iterate equals $x_*$; the iterates of $(x+1)/2$ from $x_0=0$ never reach $1$. Instead, it shows that a fixed number is smaller than every positive tolerance.
findings.problem: Padding. It repeats Chapter 11 ("The statement $x_n\to x_*$ does not say that the sequence ever reaches its limit") and the sentence just before it ("we have shown that it is smaller than every positive $\eps$"). It also interrupts the run from Step 4 to Step 5.
findings.fix: Delete the paragraph. The intuition sentence proposed for the start of Step 4 covers the useful part.

findings.quote: Recall where this bound comes from. To get from $x_n$ to $x_m$, we pass through the intermediate iterates $x_{n+1},\ldots,x_{m-1}$. The triangle inequality, used once for each intermediate point, bounds $d(x_m,x_n)$ by the total length of the single steps. Step~1 bounds each step, and the geometric sum bounds the total:
findings.problem: This recap re-derives Proposition ch11:prop:geometric-cauchy, which Chapter 11 proves and comments on ("Notice the roles of the two indices"). Keep the display as a reminder, but tighten the text around it so that Step 2 does not read like a second proof.

Since $q^n\to0$, this bound is smaller than any given tolerance once $n$ is large enough, and that is why the sequence is Cauchy." with "However far beyond $x_n$ the sequence goes, it stays within $Dq^n/(1-q)$ of $x_n$, and this bound tends to $0$ as $n$ grows; that is why the sequence is Cauchy."

findings.quote: It uses the step lengths actually observed rather than a prediction made at the start, so later in a computation it is usually far sharper than the a priori estimate.
findings.problem: "usually far sharper" undersells a fact that is easy to prove: the a posteriori bound is never weaker than the a priori bound. Step 1 gives d(x_n,x_{n-1}) <= q^{n-1}D, so q/(1-q) d(x_n,x_{n-1}) <= q^n D/(1-q).
findings.fix: It uses the step length actually observed rather than a prediction made at the start. It is never weaker than the a priori estimate, because Step~1 gives $d(x_n,x_{n-1})\le q^{n-1}D$ and therefore $\frac{q}{1-q}\,d(x_n,x_{n-1})\le\frac{q^nD}{1-q}$; when the actual steps are shorter than the worst case allows, it is much sharper.

findings.quote: The residual estimate \eqref{eq:residual} works in the opposite direction. We already have a candidate point $z$, found in any way we like, and we want a guarantee about its error. We do not need to know the fixed point $x_*$. We only need to compute $Tz$, which is usually easy, and then the residual $d(z,Tz)$. Dividing it by $1-q$ gives an error certificate for $z$.
findings.problem: This paragraph repeats almost word for word the residual paragraph in Section ch12:sec:theorem ("The point $z$ may come from anywhere ... The residual estimate turns one evaluation of $T$ into a guaranteed upper bound on the error of $z$"). It is five short sentences of padding.

Section~\ref{ch12:sec:example} does this for a map whose fixed point is not known in advance.
