findings.problem: One paragraph proves six claims: self-map, completeness (deferred), strict shrinking, no uniform q, no fixed point, unbounded iterates. It is too dense for a beginner. The text never says what "the ratio" is (|T(x)-T(y)|/|x-y| = 1-1/(xy)), and it does not state the conclusion that the inequality with factor q fails for the pair. The Archimedean property is used without a reference.
findings.fix: Split the paragraph that starts "For $x\ge1$ we have $T(x)>x\ge1$". Keep its first two sentences (self-map, completeness), then a paragraph break. Keep "To compare two outputs ... display ... Hence $|T(x)-T(y)|<|x-y|$ whenever $x\ne y$.", appending ": every pair of different points moves strictly closer together", then a paragraph break. Replace from "Yet no single factor" through "so the ratio is larger than $q$." with: "Yet no single factor $q<1$ works for all pairs. For $x\ne y$, the display shows that the ratio $|T(x)-T(y)|/|x-y|$ equals $1-1/(xy)$, and this creeps up towards $1$ as $x$ and $y$ grow. To see that it eventually exceeds any given $q$ with $0\le q<1$, choose an integer $k\ge1$ with $k>1/(1-q)$, which is possible by the Archimedean property (Section~\ref{ch02:sec:quantifiers}). For $x=k+1$ and $y=k$ the ratio is $1-1/(k(k+1))$. Since $k(k+1)>k>1/(1-q)$, we get $1/(k(k+1))<1-q$, so the ratio is larger than $q$, and the contraction inequality with factor $q$ fails for this pair." Then a paragraph break, and continue: "Finally, $T$ has no fixed point, since $x+1/x=x$ would require $1/x=0$. Starting from $x_0=1$, ..." (rest unchanged).

findings.quote: which has left the space, and from then on the contraction inequality, which was only assumed for points of $[0,1]$, says nothing. A correct inequality cannot make up for outputs that leave the space.
findings.problem: The real breakdown is that T may not be applied to x_2 at all, since T is used only for inputs in [0,1]. The closing aphorism is filler.
findings.fix: which has left the space, so $T$ may not be applied to it, and the contraction inequality, which holds only for points of $[0,1]$, cannot help.

findings.quote: Let $T(x)=x/2+1$, used only for inputs in $[0,1]$.
findings.problem: Optional tightening. Section ch12:sec:iteration already worked through the same failure with T(x)=(x+1)/2 on [0,1/2]: the formula contracts, but T(1/2)=3/4 leaves the interval, and the fixed point 1 lies outside it. A second map with exactly the same lesson adds a new formula and nothing else. Reusing the earlier map ties the two sections together.
findings.fix: Optional. Replace the subsection body with: "Return to the map $T(x)=(x+1)/2$ of Section~\ref{ch12:sec:iteration}, used only for inputs in $[0,1/2]$. The interval $[0,1/2]$ is nonempty and complete (Section~\ref{ch11:sec:complete}), and the contraction inequality holds with factor $1/2$. But $T(1/2)=3/4$ lies outside $[0,1/2]$, so $T$ is not a map from $[0,1/2]$ to itself. The only real solution of $(x+1)/2=x$ is $x=1$, which lies outside $[0,1/2]$, so $T$ has no fixed point in the interval. The proof breaks down already in Step~1: starting from $x_0=0$, we get $x_1=1/2$ and then $x_2=3/4$, which has left the space, so $T$ may not be applied to it." Change the table cell "$x/2+1$ on $[0,1]$" to "$(x+1)/2$ on $[0,1/2]$". In the Week 12 solution 12.4, rewrite the last example paragraph accordingly: "\emph{The map $(x+1)/2$ on $[0,1/2]$: the self-map condition fails.} The interval $[0,1/2]$ is nonempty, and it is complete because every closed interval is (Section~\ref{ch11:sec:complete}). For all $x,y\in[0,1/2]$, $|T(x)-T(y)|=|x-y|/2$, so the contraction inequality holds with factor $1/2$. But $T(1/2)=3/4$ does not lie in $[0,1/2]$, so $T$ is not a map from $[0,1/2]$ to itself."

findings.quote: The requirements of completeness and of the contraction inequality then hold vacuously, in the sense of Section~\ref{ch02:sec:contrapositive}, because there is nothing to check.
findings.problem: A student will ask whether there even is a map T from the empty set to itself, and whether the self-map hypothesis holds. Chapter 3 never discusses the empty map. The sentence lists only two of the three other hypotheses.
findings.fix: A map $T:X\to X$ then has no inputs to send anywhere, and the self-map condition, the contraction inequality and completeness all hold vacuously, in the sense of Section~\ref{ch02:sec:contrapositive}, because there is nothing to check.

findings.quote: The construction guarantees $m/2$ crossing edges, but it does not always find a largest cut. On the graph with vertices $a,b,c,d$ and edges $ab$, $bc$, $cd$, placing the vertices in the order $a,d,b,c$ and breaking ties by choosing the left side gives $L=\{a,c,d\}$ and $R=\{b\}$, a cut of size $2$. The cut $L=\{a,c\}$, $R=\{b,d\}$ is better: all three edges cross it.
findings.problem: Order of ideas: this example of the construction failing comes BEFORE the student has seen the construction run step by step (the triangle trace comes after it), and it gives no steps, so a beginner cannot check the claimed outcome (a and d are both ties; c is a tie between b and d). Also, the solution to Exercise 13.3 calls this 'the path example', but the text never uses the word 'path' for it, so the student cannot find what the solution refers to. (Result verified: the greedy run gives L={a,c,d}, R={b}, size 2; the cut {a,c}/{b,d} has size 3.)
findings.fix:
Delete this paragraph from its current place and put the following paragraph at the end of the section, after the triangle trace, in place of the paragraph beginning 'Notice how the three quantities behaved' (see separate finding):

"The construction guarantees $m/2$ crossing edges, but it does not always find a largest cut. Take the graph with vertices $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ and edges $ab$, $bc$, $cd$, which can be drawn as a single path $a$--$b$--$c$--$d$. Place the vertices in the order $a$, $d$, $b$, $c$, breaking ties by choosing the left side. Vertices $a$ and $d$ have no placed neighbors, so both go on the left. Vertex $b$ has $\ell=1$ (namely $a$) and $r=0$, so it goes on the right. Vertex $c$ has $\ell=1$ (namely $d$) and $r=1$ (namely $b$), a tie, so it goes on the left. The result is $L=\{a,c,d\}$, $R=\{b\}$, a cut of size $2$, because $cd$ does not cross. The cut $L=\{a,c\}$, $R=\{b,d\}$ is better: all three edges cross it."

findings.quote: Notice how the three quantities behaved. The count $C$ of settled crossing edges never went down, and the count $U$ of unsettled edges never went up. The score $F$ combines them, and the rule kept it from decreasing: it was $3/2$ at the start and after placing $a$, then $2$ after placing $b$ and after placing $c$. At the end nothing was left unsettled, and $F$ was no longer an expectation about choices still to be made but the actual size of the cut.
findings.problem: Padding: a summary that restates the trace just given and the facts already stated in 'The score of a partial placement'. Worse, the remarks that C never went down and U never went up hold for ANY placement rule, so a beginner may wrongly think the rule is responsible for them.
findings.fix: Replace the whole paragraph with the relocated example paragraph from the previous finding. If a one-line wrap-up is wanted before it, use: "The score went $3/2$, $3/2$, $2$, $2$: it never decreased, and at the end it equals the size of the cut."

findings.quote: No cut of $G$ has size $4$: for that, the three edges $ab$, $bc$, and $ca$ would all have to cross, so the vertices $a$, $b$, and $c$ would have to lie in three different sets, and there are only two.
findings.problem: Skipped step. 'Would have to lie in three different sets' is a compressed version of 'no two of a, b, c may share a side', and the reason this is impossible (pigeonhole: three vertices, two sets) is left unsaid. The text also never says outright that the largest cut of G therefore has size 3, which is what the next paragraph assumes ('we can find a largest cut by trying every possibility').
findings.fix: "No cut of $G$ has size $4$. For that, all three edges $ab$, $bc$, and $ca$ would have to cross, so no two of the vertices $a$, $b$, $c$ could lie in the same set. But there are only two sets, so by the pigeonhole principle two of these three vertices share a set, and the edge joining them does not cross. So the largest cut of $G$ has size $3$."

findings.quote: It did not need the crossing events of different edges to be unrelated, and in general they are not. Consider the \emph{triangle}, the graph with three vertices $a$, $b$, $c$ and the three edges $ab$, $bc$, $ca$. As we saw for the example graph $G$, these three edges can never all cross. So the event that all three cross has probability $0$, even though each of them crosses with probability $1/2$. (Any two of the three events are independent:
findings.problem: Confusing for a beginner. The paragraph says the crossing events are not 'unrelated' (a vague word that never appears again), then right away says, in parentheses, that any two of them ARE independent. A student who knows only the two-event definition of independence from Section 13.1 will read this as a contradiction. Nothing says what probability we would expect if the events were 'unrelated', so the 0 has nothing to be compared with. (Math checked: ab and bc both cross at 2 of the 8 labelings; all three cross at 0 of the 8.)
findings.fix:
Replace the whole paragraph with:
"The proof used independence only once, to find $\Prob(A_e)=1/2$ for a single edge. It never needed the crossing events of different edges to behave like separate coins, and in general they do not. Consider the \emph{triangle}, the graph with three vertices $a$, $b$, $c$ and the three edges $ab$, $bc$, $ca$. Each edge crosses with probability $1/2$. If the three crossing events behaved like three separate fair coins, all three edges would cross with probability $(1/2)^3=1/8$. But, as we saw for the example graph $G$, the three edges of a triangle can never all cross, so this probability is $0$. Any two of the crossing events, on the other hand, are independent in the sense of Section~\ref{ch13:sec:model}: for instance, $ab$ and $bc$ both cross exactly when $b$ gets one label and $a$ and $c$ get the other, which happens at $2$ of the $8$ labelings, and $2/8=(1/2)(1/2)$. The dependence shows up only when all three edges are considered together. Linearity of expectation does not care about any of this: the expected number of crossing edges is still $1/2+1/2+1/2=3/2$."

findings.quote: Read the theorem and its proof carefully. The expected size of the cut is $m/2$, but this does not mean that a random labeling gives a cut of size about $m/2$. Labeling every vertex $0$ gives a cut of size $0$, and that labeling is one of the possible outcomes.
findings.problem: 'Read the theorem and its proof carefully' is filler. The next sentence is vague and can mislead: for many large graphs a random labeling does give a cut close to m/2 most of the time. The real point is that the expectation promises nothing about EVERY labeling, and the all-0 labeling is the counterexample.
findings.fix: "The expected size of the cut is $m/2$, but this is not a promise about every labeling: labeling every vertex $0$ gives a cut of size $0$, and that labeling is one of the possible outcomes." (Keep the following sentences, starting 'What the argument guarantees is only...'.)

findings.quote: Choose a student uniformly at random, and let $X$ be that student's score.
findings.problem: The phrase 'uniformly at random' is never defined. Section 13.1 defines only 'the uniform model'. A student reading alone may not connect the two, and this connection is exactly what makes E X equal the class average.
findings.fix: "Choose a student at random, with every student equally likely (that is, use the uniform model on the set of students), and let $X$ be that student's score."

findings.quote: By the rule at the end of the discussion of complements in Section~\ref{ch13:sec:model}, some outcome of positive probability lies outside the union.
findings.problem: This is a clumsy pointer. The student has to go back and hunt for 'the rule at the end of the discussion of complements', when the rule could be restated in a single clause right here.
findings.fix: "An event of probability less than $1$ always leaves out some outcome of positive probability (Section~\ref{ch13:sec:model}), so some outcome of positive probability lies outside the union."

findings.quote: The group for the value $x_i$ is the sum of the terms $p(\omega)x_i$ over the outcomes with $X(\omega)=x_i$. Taking out the common factor $x_i$ leaves the sum of the probabilities of these outcomes, so the group equals $x_i\Prob(X=x_i)$.
findings.problem: This paragraph is dense: it moves from a concrete example to a general regrouping argument that is given only in words. A beginner follows sums more easily when they are displayed. The paragraph also runs the two-coin example and the general argument together.
findings.fix:
Start a new paragraph at "Combining terms in this way works in general." Replace the quoted two sentences with: "The group for the value $x_i$ consists of the terms $p(\omega)x_i$ with $X(\omega)=x_i$, and taking out the common factor $x_i$ gives
\[
\sum_{\omega:\,X(\omega)=x_i}p(\omega)\,x_i=x_i\sum_{\omega:\,X(\omega)=x_i}p(\omega)=x_i\,\Prob(X=x_i).
\]
Every outcome lies in exactly one group, so adding the groups gives back $\E X$:"

findings.quote: Because of this formula, a random variable is often described just by listing its values and their probabilities, as in ``a random variable that equals $0$ or $2$, each with probability $1/2$.'' Any finite probability space that produces these values with these probabilities gives the same expectation.
findings.problem: Three ideas share one paragraph: checking the formula on two coins, the link to the space {0,1,2}, and the convention of describing a random variable by its values and their probabilities. The convention matters later (Exercise 13.1, and the ±100 example in Section 13.6) and gets lost at the end of a long paragraph.
findings.fix: Start a new paragraph here and write: "Because of this formula, we often describe a random variable just by listing its values and their probabilities, as in ``a random variable that equals $0$ or $2$, each with probability $1/2$.'' Any finite probability space that produces these values with these probabilities gives the same expectation, so for computing expectations it does not matter which space we use."

findings.quote: Since the probabilities of all the outcomes add up to $1$, the sample space cannot be empty.
findings.problem: The reason, that an empty sum is 0 and not 1, is given only two sentences later, in a different context. A student reading this sentence asks why and does not yet have the answer.
findings.fix: "The sample space cannot be empty: a sum with no terms is $0$ (Section~\ref{ch05:sec:first-induction}), not $1$." Then, in the next paragraph, shorten "because a sum with no terms is $0$ (Section~\ref{ch05:sec:first-induction})" to "because a sum with no terms is $0$".

findings.quote: Now pick some $k$ of the objects, and decide in advance which label each of them should get.
findings.problem: The count 2^{n-k} requires the k objects to be different. The cut proof in Section 13.4 depends on exactly this ('The endpoints u and v are two different vertices. So, by the rule ... with k=2'), but the rule itself never states the condition.
findings.fix: "Now pick $k$ different objects, where $0\le k\le n$, and decide in advance which label each of them should get."

findings.quote: By linearity of expectation, the expected size of the final cut would be $C+U/2=F$. In other words, $F$ is the expected final size of the cut, given the choices made so far.
findings.problem: Small gap followed by a repetition. The student has to work out alone that each settled crossing edge contributes 1 and each settled non-crossing edge contributes 0. The 'In other words' sentence then repeats what was just said. The idea that F is the expected final size is stated three times in this section (the opening paragraph, here, and the conditional-expectation sentence).
findings.fix: "The final size of the cut is the sum of the indicators of the crossing events, one for each edge. By linearity of expectation, its expected value is the sum of their probabilities: $1$ for each of the $C$ settled edges that cross, $0$ for the other settled edges, and $1/2$ for each of the $U$ unsettled edges. This sum is $C+U/2=F$." (Delete the 'In other words' sentence.)

findings.quote: This gives a simple rule: \emph{if more of the placed neighbors of $v$ are on the left, put $v$ on the right; if more are on the right, put $v$ on the left; if the numbers are equal, either side will do.} In short, put $v$ on the side opposite to the majority of its placed neighbors.
findings.problem: Redundancy: the same rule is stated three times in a row, in the long emphasized version, then 'In short', then the Proposition.
findings.fix: "So we put $v$ on the side opposite to the majority of its placed neighbors: on the right if $\ell>r$, on the left if $r>\ell$, and on either side if $\ell=r$."

findings.quote: Every step of the calculation is visible, so no further probability theory is needed.
findings.problem: The sentence is stilted and slightly defensive, and it reads as an assessment of the text itself.
findings.fix: "We will not need the general theory of conditional expectations: here everything is captured by the formula for $F$."

findings.quote: The score $F$ starts at $m/2$, never decreases, and at the end equals the size of the cut.
findings.problem: The proof does not point back to the calculation that shows F never decreases, and it does not state the conclusion.
findings.fix: "By the calculation above, each placement changes $F$ by $|\ell-r|/2\ge0$, so $F$ never decreases. It starts at $m/2$, and once every vertex is placed it equals the size of the cut. So the cut has size at least $m/2$."

findings.quote: Sort the edges that have $v$ as an endpoint into three kinds, and see how the contribution of each one to $F$ changes if we place $v$ on the left.
findings.problem: The first two bullets claim that the edges 'were unsettled' without saying why. The reason, that v itself has not been placed yet, is easy but worth one clause for a beginner.
findings.fix: "Before $v$ is placed, every edge at $v$ is unsettled, because $v$ itself has not been placed, so each such edge contributes $1/2$ to $F$. Sort these edges into three kinds, and see how the contribution of each one changes if we place $v$ on the left." (Then the bullets can drop 'were unsettled, so each contributed $1/2$' and 'also contributed $1/2$ each'.)

findings.quote: The proof also covers a graph with no edges. Then $m/2=0$, and every cut has size at least $0$.
findings.problem: This is padding. The two sentences do not say how the proof covers the case. They only observe that the theorem is trivial there, which no beginner needs spelled out. They also break the flow between the proof and the important warning paragraph that follows.
findings.fix: Delete both sentences.

findings.quote: \begin{proposition}\label{ch13:prop:above-average}

findings.quote: as the path example in Section~\ref{ch13:sec:construction} shows, it does not always do so.

findings.quote: The reason is that if $X(\omega)<\E X$ at every outcome of positive probability, then the weighted average of these values, which is $\E X$ itself, would also lie strictly below $\E X$, which is impossible. findings.fix: Delete the sentence.

findings.problem: The sentence makes one point twice ('not itself a value' and 'not a possible result').
findings.fix: "The expectation $3/2$ itself is not a value of the variable."

findings.quote: Knowing that the aperiodic correlations are small says little about whether the periodic ones are zero.
findings.problem: This sentence clashes with Section 7. There the book states the classical fact that for even n>2, a Barker sequence (all |A_s|<=1) automatically has C_s=0 at every nonzero shift. So for even lengths, small aperiodic correlations say a great deal about the periodic ones. The only evidence offered is an odd-length example, and at odd lengths every sequence has C_s nonzero anyway (the pause just below). The next sentence, 'an argument that passes from one kind of correlation to the other has to cross it explicitly', is also stilted.
findings.fix: Replace the sentence and the closing 'bridge' sentence of the paragraph with: "Small aperiodic correlations do not by themselves make the periodic ones zero. Take the Barker sequence $(1,1,1,-1,1)$ of length five. You can check that its aperiodic correlations are $A_1=0$, $A_2=1$, $A_3=0$, and $A_4=1$. By \eqref{eq:periodaperiod}, two of its periodic correlations are $C_1=A_1+A_4=1$ and $C_2=A_2+A_3=1$, and neither is zero. (For even lengths the link is much closer, as Section~\ref{ch14:sec:research} explains.) Any argument that moves from one kind of correlation to the other has to go through equation~\eqref{eq:periodaperiod}."

findings.quote: Every pattern in the table agrees with what we have proved, and each one has a reason.
findings.problem: This overclaims. The three bullets explain only the last column and the evenness of the counts. The most visible pattern in the Barker column is that there are no Barker sequences at lengths 6, 8, 9, 10 and 12, and nothing proved in the chapter explains it. Section 7 only quotes, without proof, the facts about odd lengths and even lengths. A reader is told every pattern has a reason here, yet none is given for this one.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Three patterns in the table agree with what we have proved, and we can give a reason for each." After the itemize, optionally add: "The Barker column has a pattern of its own: there are no Barker sequences of lengths $6$, $8$, $9$, $10$, and $12$. Nothing proved in this chapter explains this; Section~\ref{ch14:sec:research} describes what is known."

findings.quote: This conclusion has no short certificate.
findings.problem: As a general statement this is false. Many lengths have very short proofs of nonexistence. Length 8 is ruled out because 8 is not a perfect square, and every odd length n>=3 is ruled out by the parity argument. The true point is narrower: an exhaustive search that finds nothing does not itself produce anything short that a reader can check independently.
findings.fix: Replace with: "The search itself leaves behind no short certificate of this conclusion. (Some lengths do have short proofs of nonexistence, such as length $8$, which is not a perfect square, but the search does not supply one.)" Keep the following sentence ("To accept it, we must trust ...") as it is.

findings.quote: being a perfect square is a \emph{necessary} condition for the order of a circulant Hadamard matrix.
findings.problem: The phrasing is imprecise. Chapter 2 defines a necessary condition Q for a statement P, and here P is 'n is the order of a circulant Hadamard matrix'. The sentence names neither P nor Q clearly.
findings.fix: Replace with: "being a perfect square is a \emph{necessary} condition for a positive integer $n$ to be the order of a circulant Hadamard matrix: if such a matrix of order $n$ exists, then $n$ is a perfect square."

findings.quote: Length $60$ alone has $2^{60}$ sign sequences, which is more than $10^{18}$. A computer that examined a billion sequences per second would need more than $36$ years for that single length.
findings.problem: The numbers are correct: 2^60 is about 1.15e18, which takes 36.5 years at 1e9 per second. But Proposition 14.7 has already shown that only the orders 16, 36, 64, ... matter for the circulant question. Length 60 is irrelevant to that question, while 16 (65,536 sequences) and 36 (about 69 seconds at a billion per second) are easy to search. An attentive reader may then doubt the claim that the search cannot 'be pushed much further'. The first order that is truly out of reach makes the point better.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Length $64$, one of the orders that Proposition~\ref{thm:circulantnecessary} leaves open, alone has $2^{64}$ sign sequences, which is more than $1.8\cdot10^{19}$. A computer that examined a billion sequences per second would need more than $580$ years for that single length." (Checked: 2^64/10^9 s = 584.5 years.)

findings.quote: and whether such a sequence exists was likewise an open question.
findings.problem: The tense is inconsistent. The first paragraph says the conjecture 'has been open since the 1960s', and the last paragraph stresses that nothing in the chapter establishes the 2026 claim. The past tense 'was' implies the question is now settled.
findings.fix: Replace with: "and whether such a sequence exists has likewise been an open question for decades."

findings.quote: This is why every count in the table of Section~\ref{ch14:sec:experiment} is even.}
findings.problem: The step is incomplete. That negation preserves both properties does not by itself make the counts even. One also needs -a to differ from a, so that the qualifying sequences split into pairs. The main text gives this step, but the solution presents the exercise alone as the reason.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Moreover $-a\ne a$, because their first entries $a_0$ and $-a_0$ differ. So the qualifying sequences of each length come in pairs $\{a,-a\}$, which is why every count in the table of Section~\ref{ch14:sec:experiment} is even.}"

findings.quote: There are Hadamard matrices of order $8$, for example, but none of them is circulant.
findings.problem: The book never shows that a Hadamard matrix of order 8 exists, so the student has to take it on trust. An explicit example is easy to give and to check.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Hadamard matrices of order $8$ do exist: if $H$ is the matrix of order four from Section~\ref{ch14:sec:circulant}, the $8$-by-$8$ matrix whose top half is $H$ next to $H$ and whose bottom half is $H$ next to $-H$ has orthogonal rows, as you can check. But $8$ is not a perfect square, so none of these matrices is circulant." (Checked: (h_i,h_i)·(h_j,h_j)=2h_i·h_j, (h_i,-h_i)·(h_j,-h_j)=2h_i·h_j, (h_i,h_i)·(h_j,-h_j)=0.)

findings.quote: the map $j\mapsto(j-i)\bmod n$ is a bijection from $\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$ to itself, and its inverse is $k\mapsto(k+i)\bmod n$.
findings.problem: The inverse is stated but never checked, and this fact is reused several times: in the dot-product computation, in Section 4, and in the solution to 14.4. A beginner may not see why the two maps undo each other.
findings.fix: Append: "To check this, note that $\bigl((j-i)\bmod n\bigr)+i$ is congruent to $j$ modulo $n$, and $j$ already lies in $\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$, so its remainder is $j$ itself; the same reasoning shows that applying the two maps in the other order also gives back the starting value."

findings.quote: Congruent integers have the same remainder on division by $n$ (Section~\ref{ch06:sec:residues}), so
findings.problem: Section ch06:sec:residues never states this fact in these words. It proves that each residue class contains exactly one of 0,...,m-1 and that an integer's remainder lies in its class, and the fact follows from these. A reader who looks up the reference will not find the sentence.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Congruent integers have the same remainder on division by $n$: both remainders lie in the same residue class and in the list $0,1,\ldots,n-1$, and by Section~\ref{ch06:sec:residues} a class contains only one member of that list. So"

findings.quote: Moreover $n\ne2$, because $2$ is not the square of an integer: $1^2=1<2<4=2^2$.
findings.problem: The check covers only nonnegative integers. Here r may be negative, and a beginner may wonder about r=-1 or r=-2.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Moreover $n\ne2$, because $2$ is not the square of an integer: since $r^2=|r|^2$, it would be the square of one of the nonnegative integers $0,1,2,\ldots$, whose squares $0,1,4,\ldots$ skip over $2$."

findings.quote: The third row is $(-1,1,1,-1)$.
findings.problem: Section 3 numbers rows from 0, and the example also says 'columns 1 and 2 (counting from 0)'. Here the ordinal 'third row' means row 2, so the reader has to switch between ordinals and 0-based indices inside one example.
findings.fix: Replace with: "The third row (row $2$, counting from $0$) is $(-1,1,1,-1)$."

findings.quote: Neither one alone would show that the two conditions are equivalent.
findings.problem: This only repeats the two sentences before it ('Both observations are needed. The first gives ... the second gives ...').
findings.fix: Delete the sentence.

findings.quote: In September 2026, a preprint claiming a proof of the circulant Hadamard conjecture was released in OpenAI's public mathematics repository,
findings.problem: The word 'preprint' is used here for the first time in the book but is not defined until Chapter 17 (17-unfamiliar-proofs/08-..., line 2). A first-year student does not know what it means, and it matters here: whether the claim has been reviewed is exactly the point.
findings.fix: In September 2026, a \emph{preprint} (a research paper made public before a journal has reviewed it) claiming a proof of the circulant Hadamard conjecture was released in OpenAI's public mathematics repository,

findings.quote: You know what a circulant matrix is, how the orthogonality of its rows translates into periodic correlations, why even-length Barker sequences belong to the same story, and exactly which orders an elementary argument leaves open.
findings.problem: This claims more than the chapter gives. The link between even-length Barker sequences and circulant Hadamard matrices is stated in the previous paragraph with 'We do not prove this here', so the student does not know *why*. The paragraph also repeats the 16, 36, 64 point from the end of Section 5 and from Section 6.
findings.fix: Replace the whole last paragraph with: "These claims come from an outside source, and nothing in this chapter establishes them: our experiment stops at length $13$, and Proposition~\ref{thm:circulantnecessary} still permits the orders $16,36,64,\ldots$. Ruling out those orders takes far more mathematics than this course covers. What the chapter does give you is the ability to read the claims precisely. You know what a circulant matrix is, how the orthogonality of its rows translates into periodic correlations, and exactly which orders our elementary argument leaves open. When you meet a summary of a result like this, whether in a news report or from an AI assistant, first check which statement was proved: which matrices, which kind of correlation, which lengths. Chapter~\ref{ch:bridge} returns to this example and describes how to begin reading a proof whose background you do not yet have."

findings.quote: We do not prove this here, but you can see one instance of it in the table.
findings.problem: The table shows only two counts (8 and 8). It does not show that the two sets of sequences are the same, so a student cannot 'see' the instance there. The student also gets no hint of why the claim might be true or why n>2 is needed, even though equation (14.1) and the parity fact from Section 1 already give half of it. The paragraph also ends in the past tense ('was likewise an open question'), which clashes with 'has been open since the 1960s' in paragraph 1.
findings.fix: Replace from "It has long been known that when $n>2$ is even" to the end of the paragraph with: "It has long been known that when $n>2$ is even, every Barker sequence of length $n$ also has $C_s=0$ for every shift $s$ with $1\le s\le n-1$, so its circulant matrix is a Hadamard matrix. Equation~\eqref{eq:periodaperiod} gives half of this at once: when $n$ and $s$ are both even, $n-s$ is even too, so a Barker sequence has $A_s=A_{n-s}=0$ (Section~\ref{ch14:sec:aperiodic}) and hence $C_s=0$. The odd shifts need a further argument, which we do not give here. The condition $n>2$ matters, because $(1,1)$ is a Barker sequence with $C_1=2A_1=2$. You can check one instance by hand. The eight Barker sequences of length four are $(1,1,1,-1)$, its three other rotations, and the negatives of these four, and they are exactly the eight sequences counted in the last column of the table. So a Barker sequence of even length greater than $4$ would give a circulant Hadamard matrix of order greater than $4$, and the even-length Barker question has stayed open for just as long." (Checked with python3: the sets coincide at n=4; (1,1) gives C_1=2.)

findings.quote: The table is evidence about these thirteen lengths and no others. It cannot rule out a qualifying sequence of some larger length that was never tested.
findings.problem: The paragraph mixes up two different reasons. The 36-year estimate shows the search is impractical. But 'More computing power is therefore not a way to settle the question for every length' does not follow from it; the real reason is that there are infinitely many lengths. The first two sentences say the same thing twice, and 'qualifying' is not defined. Section 4 makes the same point again in its paragraph 'Notice what kind of statement this is...' (see the separate finding).
findings.fix: Replace the whole paragraph with: "The table tells us about these thirteen lengths and no others. Nor can the search be pushed much further, because each additional position doubles the number of sequences. Length $60$ alone has $2^{60}$ sign sequences, which is more than $10^{18}$; a computer that examined a billion sequences per second would need more than $36$ years for that single length. And even an unlimited computer could check only finitely many lengths, while there are infinitely many. Only a proof that never uses a particular value of $n$, like the arguments of Sections~\ref{ch14:sec:square} and~\ref{ch14:sec:four}, can say something about every length at once." (Checked: 2^60 = 1.15e18; 2^60/1e9 s = 36.5 years.)

findings.quote: Notice what kind of statement this is. The argument never used a particular value of $n$, so it holds for every length at once. No list of computed examples, however long, could give a conclusion of that kind.
findings.problem: Padding. The proof-versus-search point is made in full in Section 6, in Exercise 14.6 and in the chapter goal. Here it is an early copy that interrupts the move from (14.2) to the pause.
findings.fix: Delete this paragraph. Its content is now in the Section 6 rewrite ('Only a proof that never uses a particular value of $n$ ... can say something about every length at once').

findings.quote: What do we get if we add up all the periodic correlations, including $C_0$? Each $C_s$ is itself a sum over $j$, so the total is a double sum of $n\cdot n=n^2$ products. A finite sum may be added in any order. So instead of adding, for each $s$, all the terms with that $s$, we may add, for each $j$, all the terms with that $j$:
findings.problem: This is the first double sum in the book, and the step of swapping the order of summation is the hard part. The concrete n=3 case that would make it visible comes only afterwards, as 'Another way to see the whole count'. So the student meets the abstract version first and gets the picture second, and the two explanations overlap. The opening question also repeats the section's first paragraph.
findings.fix: Replace the quoted sentences with the n=3 example as a grid read by columns, then the general case: "Start with length three and unknown entries $a_0,a_1,a_2$. The three periodic correlations, including $C_0$, are \begin{align*} C_0&=a_0a_0+a_1a_1+a_2a_2,\\ C_1&=a_0a_1+a_1a_2+a_2a_0,\\ C_2&=a_0a_2+a_1a_0+a_2a_1. \end{align*} Read this table by columns instead of by rows. The first column is $a_0a_0+a_0a_1+a_0a_2=a_0r$, the second is $a_1a_1+a_1a_2+a_1a_0=a_1r$, and the third is $a_2a_2+a_2a_0+a_2a_1=a_2r$. Adding the columns gives $(a_0+a_1+a_2)r=r^2$, so $C_0+C_1+C_2=r^2$. The same rearrangement works for every length. The total of all the $C_s$ is a sum of $n\cdot n=n^2$ products, and a finite sum may be added in any order. So instead of adding row by row (for each $s$, all terms with that $s$), we add column by column (for each $j$, all terms with that $j$):" Then delete the later paragraph that begins "Another way to see the whole count is to use three unknown entries $a_0,a_1,a_2$." and runs through "...and not, for example, $\sum_j a_j^2$."

findings.quote: For $(1,1,1,-1)$ the identity says $4+0+0+0=2^2$. It holds for every sequence, not only for special ones.
findings.problem: 'The identity' is never stated as a result in its own right. It sits at the end of a four-line align, after three bullets, and later text refers back to 'the left side of the identity'. A student has to hunt for it.
findings.fix:
So for every sign sequence of length $n$,
\[
C_0+C_1+\cdots+C_{n-1}=r^2.
\]
For $(1,1,1,-1)$ this says $4+0+0+0=2^2$.

findings.quote: Keeping track of which hypothesis is used where tells us which parts of the argument would still work in a more general setting.
findings.problem: A generic moral that adds nothing to the two sentences before it, which already say exactly where the sign hypothesis is used.
findings.fix: Delete the sentence.

findings.quote: \pauseq{Which lengths $n$ with $1\le n\le13$ pass the square test?
findings.problem: The bound 13 looks arbitrary: the table that stops at 13 comes only in Section 6. The name 'square test' is also new; elsewhere the text says 'square condition'.
findings.fix: \pauseq{Which lengths $n$ with $1\le n\le13$ (the lengths covered by the computer search of Section~\ref{ch14:sec:experiment}) pass the square condition, that is, are perfect squares?

findings.quote: In each overlapping position, multiply the two entries. The product $a_ja_{j+s}$ is $1$ when the two entries agree and $-1$ when they differ.
findings.problem: The symbols $a_j$ and $a_{j+s}$ appear before the text says what $j$ is or which entry of the picture each symbol names. A student looking at the two-row picture cannot tell which entry is $a_j$, so the sum in the definition seems to come from nowhere.
findings.fix: Each overlapping column holds an entry $a_j$ of the shifted copy and, directly above it, the entry $a_{j+s}$ of the original, which lies $s$ places further along the list. Multiply the two: the product $a_ja_{j+s}$ is $1$ when the entries agree and $-1$ when they differ.

findings.quote: When it is clear which sequence we mean, we write $A_s$ instead of $A_s(a)$. Since each product is $+1$ for an agreement and $-1$ for a disagreement, $A_s$ is the number of overlapping positions where the sequence agrees with its shifted copy, minus the number where it disagrees.
findings.problem: This one paragraph does six jobs: notation, the agree-minus-disagree reading (which repeats the sentence just before the definition), the prefix 'auto', the word 'aperiodic', why large shifts are left out and why shift zero is left out. It is hard to scan.
findings.fix:
Replace the paragraph with two short ones: "When it is clear which sequence we mean, we write $A_s$ instead of $A_s(a)$. In words, $A_s$ is the number of overlapping positions where the sequence agrees with its shifted copy, minus the number where it disagrees. The prefix ``auto'' means that the sequence is compared with itself, and ``aperiodic'' means that nothing wraps around: entries pushed past the end of the list simply drop off, as the last $-1$ in the picture does.

Two kinds of shift are left out. A shift of $n$ or more leaves no overlap at all. At shift zero every entry would be compared with itself, giving $a_0^2+a_1^2+\cdots+a_{n-1}^2=n$ because every sign has square one; that value is the same for every sequence of length $n$, so it tells us nothing."

findings.quote: Notice that the two kinds of subscript play different roles. The subscript on $A_s$ records a shift, whereas the subscript on $a_j$ records a position in the list. The uppercase quantity is a sum built from the lowercase entries. Keeping these roles apart helps when several indices appear in one calculation.
findings.problem: Four sentences for one point, and the third restates the definition.
findings.fix: Keep the two kinds of subscript apart: the $s$ in $A_s$ is a shift, while the $j$ in $a_j$ is a position in the list.

findings.quote: For a Barker sequence this fixes every correlation up to its sign.
findings.problem: This vague summary ('up to its sign' is not even accurate when A_s=0) comes before the two sentences that state the fact precisely.
findings.fix: Delete the sentence. The paragraph continues correctly with "The only even integer with absolute value at most one is $0$..."

findings.quote: and $C_0=4$. So every periodic correlation of this sequence at a nonzero shift is zero. Sequences with this property are what the rest of the chapter is about.
findings.problem: Awkward transition. Section 1 builds up Barker sequences, and Section 2 drops them without a word. A student will wonder why Barker sequences were introduced. They come back only in the table and in Section 7.
findings.fix: and $C_0=4$. So every periodic correlation of this sequence at a nonzero shift is zero. Sequences with this property are what the rest of the chapter is about. Barker sequences will return in Section~\ref{ch14:sec:research}, where they turn out to lead to the same question.

findings.quote: Again we write $C_s$ when the sequence is clear. Unlike $A_s$, this sum always has $n$ terms, one for each position $j$. At shift zero every entry is paired with itself, so $C_0=n$.
findings.problem: Section 1 explained at some length why shift zero is left out of $A_s$, because it 'tells us nothing'. Now shift zero is allowed for $C_s$ without comment, and an attentive student will ask why.
findings.fix: Again we write $C_s$ when the sequence is clear. Unlike $A_s$, this sum always has $n$ terms, one for each position $j$. At shift zero every entry is paired with itself, so $C_0=n$ for every sequence. That value carries no information about the sequence, but we include it this time because it appears naturally in Sections~\ref{ch14:sec:circulant} and~\ref{ch14:sec:square}.

findings.quote: Here is the same split in a concrete case, $n=5$ and $s=2$. The periodic sum has five terms, and the last two are the ones that wrap around:
findings.problem: Order of ideas: the general index change (the itemize list, the two-group sum, the substitution $k=j+s-n$) comes first and the concrete n=5, s=2 picture comes after it. A beginner needs the picture first to follow the substitution.
findings.fix: Move this paragraph, with its display and the sentence "Swapping the factors turns the last two terms into $a_0a_3+a_1a_4$, which is $A_3$.", to the start of the subsection, right after the heading. Then continue: "So $C_2=A_2+A_3$. The same split works for every shift. Fix a shift $s$ with $1\le s\le n-1$. ..." At the old location, keep only "So, for every shift $s$ with $1\le s\le n-1$," before the display of (14.1).

findings.quote: Equation~\eqref{eq:periodaperiod} is the bridge between the two notions, and an argument that passes from one kind of correlation to the other has to cross it explicitly.
findings.problem: Stilted, abstract sentence ('has to cross it explicitly') that reads like advice to an author rather than mathematics for a student.
findings.fix: Delete the sentence.

findings.quote: In the language of Section~\ref{ch03:sec:injsurj}, the map $j\mapsto(j-i)\bmod n$ is a bijection from $\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$ to itself, and its inverse is $k\mapsto(k+i)\bmod n$.
findings.problem: The inverse is stated but never checked, and this bijection is the key fact behind the change of index (it is used again in Section 4 and in Solution 14.4). A beginner cannot see why $((j-i)\bmod n+i)\bmod n=j$.
findings.fix: Append: "To check this, let $k=(j-i)\bmod n$. Then $k\equiv j-i\pmod n$, so $k+i\equiv j\pmod n$. Since $j$ already lies between $0$ and $n-1$, it is the remainder of $k+i$ on division by $n$; that is, $j=(k+i)\bmod n$. The same argument with $j$ and $k$ exchanged undoes the map in the other order."

findings.quote: Row $i$ is the sequence rotated $i$ places to the right. For instance,
findings.problem: The formula $H_{ij}=a_{(j-i)\bmod n}$ is given without saying why the index is $j-i$ and not $j+i$, which is a common point of confusion.
findings.fix: Row $i$ is the sequence rotated $i$ places to the right. Rotating moves the entry $a_k$ from column $k$ to column $k+i$ (wrapping past the end), so the entry that lands in column $j$ is the one with $k\equiv j-i$, namely $a_{(j-i)\bmod n}$. For instance,

findings.quote: Each row is the row above it with its last entry moved to the front.
findings.problem: This is the third statement of the rotation rule. It already appears in the first paragraph ('moving every entry one place to the right, with the last entry wrapping around to the front') and in 'Row i is the sequence rotated i places to the right'.
findings.fix: Delete the sentence.

findings.quote: In particular, every row has squared length $a_0^2+a_1^2+\cdots+a_{n-1}^2=n$.
findings.problem: Said twice. The subsection on HH^T makes the same point in general ('the diagonal equations hold automatically, because each row consists of n entries with square one').
findings.fix: Delete the sentence here and keep the version in the Hadamard paragraph (see the compressed replacement below).

findings.quote: Both observations are needed. The first gives the ``if'' direction of part~(b), and the second gives the ``only if'' direction. Neither one alone would show that the two conditions are equivalent.
findings.problem: This only restates the proof just above it, which already says 'By the first observation...' and 'By the second observation...'. The last sentence is filler.
findings.fix: Delete the paragraph. If you keep one sentence, use: "The first observation gives the ``if'' direction of part~(b), and the second gives the ``only if'' direction."

findings.quote: Section~\ref{ch10:sec:product} called a square matrix with entries $\pm1$ a \emph{Hadamard matrix} when it satisfies $HH^{\mathsf T}=nI$, where $n$ is the number of rows. This number is called the \emph{order} of the matrix.
findings.problem: The paragraph that starts here retells almost word for word the explanation in Section 10.6 (diagonal entries give squared length n, off-diagonal entries give orthogonality). It takes eight sentences for something a reminder can do in four.
findings.fix: Replace the whole paragraph (through "...exactly when any two different rows are orthogonal.") with: "Recall from Section~\ref{ch10:sec:product} that a square matrix $H$ with entries $\pm1$ is a \emph{Hadamard matrix} when $HH^{\mathsf T}=nI$, where $n$, the number of rows, is called the \emph{order} of $H$. This one identity packs $n^2$ equations between numbers, one for each position $(i,\ell)$: the left side is the dot product of row $i$ with row $\ell$, and the right side is $n$ if $i=\ell$ and $0$ otherwise. The diagonal equations say that every row has squared length $n$, which is automatic when the $n$ entries all have square one. So a square matrix with entries $\pm1$ is a Hadamard matrix exactly when any two different rows are orthogonal."

findings.quote: A matrix identity is useful because it collects many related equations into one line, but to understand it you have to know what a single one of its entries says.
findings.problem: A moral that repeats the subsection title. Separately, in the sentence before, '$C_{(0-1)\bmod4}=C_3$' may stop a student who computes $(0-1)\bmod 4$ as $-1$.
findings.fix: Delete the quoted sentence. In "By Proposition~\ref{ch14:prop:rows}(a) this is $C_{(0-1)\bmod4}=C_3$," add "(since $-1=(-1)\cdot4+3$)" after $C_3$.

findings.quote: The second factor must also be written in terms of $k$. Since $k\equiv j-i\pmod n$,
findings.problem: The next display adds $i-\ell$ to both sides of a congruence. A beginner may not remember that this is allowed. It was shown in Section 6.3 (well-definedness of addition).

findings.fix: \section{Circulant matrices turn correlations into dot products}\label{ch14:sec:circulant}

findings.quote: For the orders $16,36,64,\ldots$ the proposition says nothing either way. It neither builds a matrix of such an order nor rules one out. This is typical of a necessary condition: it removes most orders from consideration and tells us precisely which ones remain open. That list of remaining orders is the boundary between what our elementary arguments can decide and what needs new ideas.
findings.problem: Four sentences, where the first two say the same thing and the third repeats it in general terms.
findings.fix: For the orders $16,36,64,\ldots$ the proposition says nothing either way: it neither builds a matrix of such an order nor rules one out. These remaining orders mark the boundary between what our elementary arguments can decide and what needs new ideas.

findings.quote: (Subtracting them gives $y=0$ as well, although we will not need it.)
findings.problem: An aside the argument does not use. It slows the main line of the proof.
findings.fix: Delete the parenthetical.

findings.quote: Two kinds of change keep a matrix Hadamard.
findings.problem: 'Keep a matrix Hadamard' is clipped jargon.
findings.fix: Two kinds of change turn a Hadamard matrix into another Hadamard matrix.

findings.quote: The conjecture has been open since the 1960s.
findings.problem: Two paragraphs later the section reports a claimed proof, so 'has been open' sits uneasily with it, and the tense differs from the rest of the section.
findings.fix: The conjecture dates from the 1960s, and for decades it resisted every attempt at a proof.

findings.quote: Let $a$ be a sign sequence of length $n$. Prove that $C_{n-s}=C_s$ by renaming the summation index in the sum that defines $C_{n-s}$. For which shifts $s$ are both sides of this equation defined?
findings.problem: The exercise asks for a proof before asking where the statement makes sense. The solution already answers in the logical order (domain first, then proof), so the exercise should ask in that order too.
findings.fix: Let $a$ be a sign sequence of length $n$. For which shifts $s$ are both $C_s$ and $C_{n-s}$ defined? For each such shift, prove that $C_{n-s}=C_s$ by renaming the summation index in the sum that defines $C_{n-s}$.

findings.quote: This is why every count in the table of Section~\ref{ch14:sec:experiment} is even.
findings.problem: Incomplete reasoning. Evenness also needs $-a\ne a$, so that the sequences really pair off. Section 6 says this, but the solution claims 'This is why' without it.
findings.fix: Since $-a\ne a$ (their first entries differ), the sequences counted in each row of the table of Section~\ref{ch14:sec:experiment} come in pairs $\{a,-a\}$, which is why every count there is even.

findings.quote: The answer does not show that a circulant Hadamard matrix of order $16$ or $36$ exists. Necessary conditions can only rule orders out. Passing both tests means only that these two tests cannot exclude $16$ and $36$; neither test builds a matrix.
findings.problem: Three sentences say the same thing. Also, in the last paragraph, 'There are Hadamard matrices of order $8$, for example, but none of them is circulant.' does not say why none is circulant.
findings.fix: Replace with: "No. Necessary conditions can only rule orders out; passing both tests means only that these two tests cannot exclude $16$ and $36$." Then change the last sentence to: "For example, there are Hadamard matrices of order $8$, but none of them is circulant, because $8$ is not a perfect square."

findings.quote: A circulant Hadamard matrix of order $n$ exists exactly when some sign sequence of length $n$ has $C_s=0$ for every shift $s$ with $1\le s\le n-1$.
findings.problem: Optional tightening. The condition '$C_s=0$ for every shift $s$ with $1\le s\le n-1$' (or 'all of its periodic correlations at nonzero shifts equal to zero') appears about 19 times across the chapter and its solutions, which makes many sentences heavy. The standard term for such a sequence is 'perfect'.
findings.fix: In Section 2, after the (1,1,1,-1) example, add: "We call a sign sequence \emph{perfect} when $C_s=0$ for every shift $s$ with $1\le s\le n-1$; so $(1,1,1,-1)$ is perfect." Then use the word where the long phrase recurs, for example: "A circulant Hadamard matrix of order $n$ exists exactly when some sign sequence of length $n$ is perfect." and the table header "Perfect sequences". Keep the long form in Proposition~\ref{ch14:prop:rows}(b), since it is the precise statement. Only adopt this if it can be applied consistently.

findings.quote: and translate the question into one about matrices whose rows are orthogonal.
findings.problem: 'The question' has no antecedent: the sentence before it describes a measurement, not a question.
findings.fix: and translate the search for sequences that match none of their rotated copies into a question about matrices whose rows are orthogonal.

findings.quote: Now read the proof one line at a time. At the start, the goal is \code{P -> R}.
findings.problem: This is the first use of the technical term "goal". It is used throughout Sections 3 and 4 ("changes the goal", "the current goal"), but it is defined only at the end of the section ("shows the goal, the proposition that remains to be proved"). Chapter 4 called this the "target" or the "still to show" list, so a beginner reading alone meets an undefined term at the start of the first line-by-line reading.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Now read the proof one line at a time. Lean calls the proposition that still has to be proved the \emph{goal}; it is the ``still to show'' list of Section~\ref{ch04:sec:directions}. At the start, the goal is \code{P -> R}." Optionally shorten the later sentence to "The line that begins with $\vdash$, a symbol called the \emph{turnstile}, shows the goal."

findings.quote: The expression \code{(fun x => g (f x)) x} means ``apply the rule $x\mapsto g(f(x))$ to the input $x$,'' and evaluating that application gives \code{g (f x)}.
findings.problem: The letter x plays two different roles in this display. Inside "fun x => ..." it is a placeholder (bound variable). After the parenthesis it is the particular element introduced by "intro x y h". The text never says that the name after "fun" is only a placeholder. A beginner will find "apply the rule x->g(f(x)) to the input x" confusing or circular. The same pattern appears again in Chapter 16 as "(fun x => g (f x)) a".
findings.fix: After the quoted sentence, add: "The letter \code{x} plays two roles here. Inside \code{fun x => g (f x)} it is only a placeholder for whatever input the rule receives: \code{fun z => g (f z)} is the same function. The \code{x} after the closing parenthesis is the particular element introduced by \code{intro}. Evaluating the application puts that element in place of the placeholder."

findings.quote: Lean writes the conjunction $P\land Q$ as \code{And P Q}, and the infoview displays it as $P\land Q$.
findings.problem: This is slightly inaccurate. Lean's standard notation for conjunction is P ∧ Q, which is accepted in files and is the notation used in most Lean code. And P Q is the underlying name, which this book chooses to write. Chapter 16 itself says "In our files we write the names And, Not, and Exists instead". A student who later reads other Lean code would be misled. The same applies to "Lean writes the statement ... as \code{Exists (fun n : Nat => n + 1 = 4)}" in Section 6.
findings.fix: Replace with: "In our files we write the conjunction $P\land Q$ as \code{And P Q}, which is its name in Lean. Lean also accepts the usual symbol $\land$, and the infoview always displays the conjunction as $P\land Q$." (Tested: "P ∧ Q -> Q ∧ P" with the same proof compiles in Lean 4.19.) In Section 6, similarly change "Lean writes the statement" to "We write the statement".

findings.quote: For each function \code{f : A -> B}, it defines \code{Inj f} to be a proposition; that is what the type \code{Prop} after the last colon says.
findings.problem: The phrase "after the last colon" is ambiguous. The last colon in the displayed definition is in the body, "forall x y : A", not the one before Prop. A beginner who counts colons will look in the wrong place. Section 2 uses the clearer phrase "the statement that follows its parameters and its colon".
findings.fix: Replace "after the last colon" with "after the colon that follows the parameters".

findings.quote: Some tactics, however, look for the literal written form of an expression, and Chapter~\ref{ch:lean2} shows a case where we must first ask Lean to display the reduced form.
findings.problem: In Chapter 16 the fix is the tactic show, which replaces the goal by its reduced form. Calling this "display" suggests that only the on-screen presentation changes. If that were so, it could not affect rw, which is the whole point of the sentence.
findings.fix: Replace the end with: "... shows a case where we must first restate the goal in its reduced form, using the tactic \code{show}."

findings.quote: But when $n$ is a variable, neither side can be computed to a number, the two sides remain different expressions, and \code{rfl} fails.
findings.problem: The explanation is correct (tested: rfl fails on twice n = 2 * n). But a beginner may conclude that rfl never works when a variable is present. In fact "twice n = n + n" is proved by rfl, and Chapter 16 uses rfl on statements with variables (preimage_meet).
findings.fix: Add after the sentence: "Variables alone do not stop \code{rfl}: the equation \code{twice n = n + n} is proved by \code{rfl}, because unfolding \code{twice} turns the left side into exactly the right side." (Tested in Lean 4.19: "theorem twice_eq_add (n : Nat) : twice n = n + n := by rfl" compiles.)

findings.quote: Start & \code{hpq : P -> Q} and \code{hqr : Q -> R} & \code{P -> R}\\
findings.problem: The column is headed "Fact added", but at the start nothing is added. The listed facts are the parameters, and the list omits P Q R : Prop, which the infoview display shown just below lists as its first line.
findings.fix: Change the row to: "Start & the parameters \code{P Q R : Prop}, \code{hpq : P -> Q}, \code{hqr : Q -> R} & \code{P -> R}\\".

findings.quote: Here is the first half of Exercise~\ref{ex:3.5}: a function with a left inverse is injective.
findings.problem: In Exercise 3.5 the left inverse is the function h, with h∘f = id_A. Here the left inverse is called g, and h names the hypothesis. A reader who compares the two will be confused about what h denotes.
findings.fix: Append: "Here the left inverse is called \code{g}, and the name \code{h} is used for the hypothesis that $g\circ f$ is the identity."

findings.quote: \subsection*{The type of a number changes the available operations}
findings.problem: The subsection does not show that operations become unavailable. It shows that the same symbol "-" names a different operation depending on the type. The subsection also starts abruptly inside a section about existence, with no link to what came before.
findings.fix: Retitle to "\subsection*{The type of a number decides what its operations mean}". Begin the first paragraph with: "The witness above had to be a natural number, because the statement declared \code{n : Nat}. The type of a number matters in another way too."

findings.quote: The input to \code{Exists} is a function that turns each natural number $n$ into the proposition $n+1=4$, so the whole expression says that some natural number has this property.
findings.problem: Section 2 introduced fun only without a type, as "fun x => x + 1". The new form "fun n : Nat => ..." is never explained.
findings.fix: Insert before this sentence: "The part \code{n : Nat} after \code{fun} declares that the input \code{n} is a natural number."

findings.quote: If all we know is that some number has a property, we cannot yet compute with that number.
findings.problem: "Compute with" is vague and slightly off. What is missing is a name for the number, so that it can be referred to at all.
findings.fix: Replace with: "If all we know is that some number has a property, we have no name for that number, so we cannot yet refer to it."

findings.quote: This is the proof of Proposition~\ref{thm:compconverse} written in Lean.
findings.problem: The Lean theorem proves only the first part of Proposition 3.x. The second part, that g need not be injective, is a counterexample and is not formalized. The next sentence, "None could be required, because $g$ need not be injective.", is also awkwardly phrased.
findings.fix: Replace with "This is the proof of the first part of Proposition~\ref{thm:compconverse}, written in Lean." Replace "None could be required, because $g$ need not be injective." with "Nor could it use one: by the second part of Proposition~\ref{thm:compconverse}, $g$ need not be injective."

findings.quote: Moving the cursor through the proof line by line and comparing the infoview with the table is a good way to learn to read proof states.
findings.problem: This repeats almost word for word the advice at the end of Section 1 ("move the cursor through each proof one line at a time and compare the proof state in the infoview with the explanation in the text").
findings.fix: Shorten to: "Try this with the cursor: step through the three lines and check that the infoview agrees with each row of the table." Alternatively, delete the sentence.
